findings.title: Rebasing stETH held by the PoolManager gains and loses balance outside pool accounting
findings.difference: stETH balances are recalculated on each Lido oracle report, normally daily, with no transfer. The change is positive on staking rewards and can be negative after slashing or penalties. Lido's integration guide lists Uniswap among applications that are not designed for rebasing tokens and recommends wstETH.
findings.mechanism: Pool accounting never reads token balances. Balances are read only in sync and in _settle, and the only credit from a balance is the increase between a sync and the settle that follows in the same transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). A positive rebase raises balanceOf(PoolManager) with no sync and settle around it, so the increase belongs to no pool, no position and no claim. The only outflows are take and collectProtocolFees (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), and both debit an accounted amount, so the surplus cannot be paid out to LPs. Someone who can run sync, the rebase and settle inside one transaction would be credited the whole rebase on the PoolManager's balance. For stETH the rebase happens inside submitReportData, which only an oracle committee member or a SUBMIT_DATA_ROLE holder can call. A negative rebase lowers the balance below the sum of pool and claim accounting, and the last withdrawals of stETH revert in Currency.transfer. Transfer rounding is safe for the PoolManager: a take debits the full amount while stETH moves at most that amount, and settle credits what arrived.
findings.impact: The PoolManager holds 80.4539 stETH at block 26470360. LPs in stETH pools earn no staking yield on it; the yield accumulates as an unclaimable surplus. After a negative rebase the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws stETH last. wstETH (2,295 held) is not affected because its balances do not rebase.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use stETH or another elastic supply token as a currency. The loss case needs a negative Lido report. Capturing the positive rebase needs an oracle committee member acting through a contract or an EIP-7702 delegated account. I derived the rounding argument from the share formula in the Lido guide and did not test it on chain. I did not compute how much of the 80.4539 stETH is surplus.
findings.mitigations: Use wstETH in pools. Interfaces can warn on pools whose currency is stETH or another rebasing token. A hook cannot fix this because the surplus is not reachable through any delta.

verification.factCheck: The Lido integration guide says stETH balances are recalculated when the oracle reports, normally daily, that a rebase can be negative after slashing or penalties, that transfers can move 1 to 2 wei less than requested, and that Maker, UniSwap and SushiSwap are not designed for rebasable tokens so holders there may not receive their daily rewards. The same guide says daily rebases had never been negative at the time of writing. The accounting oracle page says submitReportData reverts with SenderNotAllowed unless the caller holds SUBMIT_DATA_ROLE or is a consensus member, and that this call triggers the rebase. On chain at block 26470974 stETH.balanceOf(PoolManager) was 80.468369861 and sharesOf was 64.380487063, which is 1.2498875596 stETH per share. The researcher recorded 80.453883612 and 64.372946869 at block 26470380, which is 1.2498089263 per share. The rate rose by 0.0063 percent between the two readings. That matches one daily report at about 2.3 percent a year and added about 0.005 stETH to the PoolManager's balance on the earlier shares with no transfer. The public RPC refused archive calls, so I could not read the earlier block myself. The earlier figures are the researcher's.
verification.codeCheck: balanceOfSelf is called only in sync (src/PoolManager.sol:285) and in _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:359). currency.transfer is called only in take (src/PoolManager.sol:295) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). take debits the caller's delta by the full amount, and collection is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued with a checked subtraction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-55). A balance increase that has no sync before it and no settle after it therefore reaches no delta and cannot be paid out. A caller who runs sync, then the rebase, then settle in one transaction is credited the whole increase on the PoolManager's balance (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364), and sync needs no unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:279). For stETH only an oracle member or a SUBMIT_DATA_ROLE holder can place the rebase inside such a transaction. After a negative rebase the balance is below the sum of deltas that pools and claims can produce, and the last take reverts in Currency.transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). I checked the rounding argument from the share formula: a transfer moves floor(amount * totalShares / totalPooledEther) shares, so the sender's balance falls by at most the amount that take debited. I did not test it on chain. No test in test/ models a rebasing token.
verification.corrections: I raise the severity from low to medium. Low is for hazards with no direct loss path. Here the staking yield on stETH held by the PoolManager is stranded for good, the increase is visible on chain, and the loss is limited to stETH pools and claims, which is the medium definition. The effect is closer to a permanent freeze of the yield than to degrade. The principal shortfall case needs a negative report, which the Lido guide says had not happened when it was written. The same sync, trigger, settle sequence applies to any token whose balance at the PoolManager a third party can raise inside one transaction, which is recorded as a lead.

findings.title: A take to a recipient whose receive policy rejects the PoolManager succeeds and strands the funds in ReceivePolicyGuard
findings.difference: Since T6 any Tempo account can set a receive policy in the TIP-403 registry: a sender list, a token filter and a recovery authority. When a TIP-20 transfer fails the recipient's receive policy, the transfer does not revert. The token credits ReceivePolicyGuard at 0xB10C000000000000000000000000000000000000, records a receipt and returns true. Only the recovery authority captured in the receipt can claim the amount. With recovery authority address(0) the claimer is the originator, which is the from address of the transfer. An ERC-20 transfer on Ethereum either credits the recipient or reverts.
findings.mechanism: 1. A user or a router calls take(currency, to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The caller's delta is debited and the PoolManager calls transfer(to, amount) on the TIP-20 (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). 2. The recipient to has a receive policy that rejects the PoolManager as sender, or filters out the token. The TIP-20 precompile moves the amount from the PoolManager to ReceivePolicyGuard with the PoolManager as originator and returns true. 3. The return value is 32 bytes of 1, so the success test at src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 passes and take completes. The recipient's balance is unchanged. 4. If the recipient's recovery authority is its own address or a third party, that party can claim. If it is address(0), only the originator can claim. The originator is the PoolManager, which has no function that calls the guard, so the receipt can never be claimed. 5. PoolManager accounting stays consistent, because the delta was debited and the balance fell by the same amount. The loss is the withdrawing party's.
findings.impact: The amount of each affected take is lost for good when the recipient's recovery authority is address(0), and delayed until a claim otherwise. This hits LP withdrawals and swap outputs sent to accounts that restrict senders, for example custodial deposit accounts with a sender whitelist. Pool reserves and other users are not affected.
findings.preconditions: The recipient must have set a receive policy that rejects the PoolManager address or the token, and must have chosen address(0) as recovery authority for the loss to be permanent. The party that names the recipient in take must not check the policy first. An attacker cannot set a policy for someone else. receivePolicy(PoolManager) is unset on chain, and the PoolManager cannot set one, so payments into the PoolManager are not redirected.
findings.mitigations: Routers and interfaces on Tempo should call validateReceivePolicy(token, PoolManager, recipient) before a take and refuse or warn when it would block. Account owners who use sender whitelists should add the PoolManager address or set themselves as recovery authority. The deployer can document that withdrawals originate from the PoolManager address.

verification.factCheck: The receive policies page states that a blocked inbound TIP-20 transfer still succeeds, that delivery goes to ReceivePolicyGuard at 0xB10C000000000000000000000000000000000000, and that with recovery authority address(0) only the transfer originator may claim. The TIP-20 specification says a receiver policy rejection must not revert the transfer. In the client source, transfer returns Ok(true) when validate_transfer reports a blocked inbound, validate_inbound_or_block moves the amount from the originator to the guard, and for transfer the originator is msg.sender. claim in the guard reverts with unauthorized_claimer unless msg.sender equals the recovery authority resolved from the receipt. I tested it on chain. I read the ReceivePolicyUpdated logs of the registry over the last 30,000,000 blocks and found 19 events. Two accounts, 0xec0eca588024e2d0091e74bd9034ff581111ea7f and 0x5bfa9123fa9dc6448d24ebbdb59e98f237de70c3, have sender policy 0, which rejects every sender. validateReceivePolicy(OUSD, PoolManager, account) returns 2 for both. An eth_simulateV1 of OUSD.transfer(account, 1) from the PoolManager address returns true and emits Transfer from the PoolManager to the guard and TransferBlocked from the guard. Afterwards the guard's balance is up by 1, the recipient's balance is unchanged and the PoolManager's balance is down by 1. The guard's functions are claim(address,bytes) with selector 0xbb1757cf, balanceOf(bytes) and burnBlockedReceipt(bytes). eth_call from the PoolManager address to the guard with transfer(address,uint256) and balanceOf(address) reverts with an unknown selector error.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller's delta and calls transfer(to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The success test accepts a 32 byte return value of 1 (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), which is what the TIP-20 returns for a redirected transfer, so take completes. Nothing in take reads the recipient's balance. The debit and the balance drop are equal, so PoolManager accounting stays whole and the loss falls on the party that named the recipient. The PoolManager makes outbound calls with four kinds of selector only: transfer(address,uint256) at src/types/Currency.sol:60-73, balanceOf(address) at src/types/Currency.sol:94, unlockCallback(bytes) to its caller at src/PoolManager.sol:110, and hook selectors to addresses with flag bits (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-134). The guard address has no flag bits and none of these selectors is claim, so a receipt whose originator is the PoolManager cannot be claimed. The tests have no token that returns true without crediting the recipient.
verification.corrections: The mechanism holds as written. Two points on reach. First, both accounts that reject all senders today name themselves as recovery authority, so they could claim a redirected amount. Three accounts have chosen address(0) as recovery authority, and all three currently allow every sender and every token. I found no account that is in the permanent loss configuration today. Second, a router that takes to itself and then forwards becomes the originator, and a router has no claim function either. The Universal Router and PositionManager on Tempo were not read. The severity stays medium. No third party can trigger the loss, pool reserves are not in reach, and the amount is limited to takes sent to accounts that set such a policy.

findings.title: Any account can book a balance increase it triggers at the PoolManager as its own payment, and EIP-7702 removes the origin check that guards Ampleforth's public rebase
findings.difference: Mainnet is the reference chain, so the difference is one that arrived after the Dencun rules the build targets. Since Pectra (EIP-7702) an EOA can run code and still satisfy msg.sender == tx.origin. The Ampleforth Orchestrator on mainnet uses that check as its only guard on the public rebase() function, and its source says the guard exists to protect liquidity providers from flash loan attacks. Mainnet also has reward contracts that pay a holder when any third party asks, such as Compound's claimComp(holder).
findings.mechanism: sync has no lock check and records balanceOf(PoolManager) for any currency (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). _settle credits the named recipient with the whole rise in that balance since the sync (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). Pool accounting never reads balances, so a rise that comes from a rebase or a reward payment belongs to no pool, position or claim until someone settles it. The steps for AMPL are these. The attacker is an EOA that has delegated to its own contract code and sends a transaction to itself. Its code calls unlock, and the PoolManager calls unlockCallback on the same EOA (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). Inside the callback the code calls sync(AMPL), then Orchestrator.rebase(), which passes the origin check because the caller is the transaction sender. When the day's supply change is positive, the AMPL balance of every holder grows, including the PoolManager's. The code then calls settle, which credits the attacker with the growth on the PoolManager's entire AMPL balance, and take(AMPL, attacker, growth), which pays it out (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). All deltas are zero and unlock returns. The attacker paid gas only. The same bracket works for any token where an ordinary account can cause a transfer or a balance increase to the PoolManager: a reward claim on behalf of a holder, an airdrop claim that pays a named account, or a rebase with a public trigger. A negative rebase is never bracketed, so liquidity providers keep the losses and lose the gains. This is the unprivileged form of the stETH finding from cycle 1, where the trigger needs an oracle member.
findings.impact: The gain of each positive rebase or reward payment on the full balance the PoolManager holds in that token, across all pools, claims and accrued protocol fees. The existing mainnet PoolManager holds 16 base units of AMPL, and the public triggers I simulated moved nothing at block 26471590 (0 COMP from claimComp, no sOHM change), so the amount at risk today is close to zero. The new deployment starts empty. The exposure grows with any pool that lists a token of this kind. Without an attacker the same increase stays in the PoolManager as a surplus that core has no function to pay out, so liquidity providers do not receive it in either case; the attacker turns a stranded amount into a taken one.
findings.preconditions: A pool or claim balance in a token whose balanceOf(PoolManager) an ordinary account can raise without paying the same amount: AMPL when a positive rebase is due and the attacker is first in the rebase window, or a token with a public reward or airdrop push to holders. For AMPL the attacker needs an EIP-7702 delegation, which any EOA can set. The rebase window is 1,200 seconds per day (offset 7,200 seconds into each 86,400), and the policy reported inRebaseWindow() = 0 at block 26471631, so my simulated rebase() call reverted. I did not execute the full sequence and did not simulate a delegated EOA; the origin check claim rests on the EIP text and the verified source. I checked 12 rebasing or reward-bearing tokens out of 66,554 token rows the explorer lists for the PoolManager.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers and interfaces can avoid or flag pools in elastic supply and reward-pushing tokens and use wrapped, non-rebasing forms. A keeper or a hook can run the same bracket first and pass the proceeds to the pool with donate (src/PoolManager.sol:256-276), which returns the increase to in-range liquidity providers. Token projects cannot rely on msg.sender == tx.origin to keep contracts out. The deployer cannot close this in core without tracking reserves per currency.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the Sourcify record for 0x6fb00a180781e75f87e2b690af0196baa77c7e7c on 22 November 2026. It reports a full creation and runtime match, contract name Orchestrator, solc 0.4.24. rebase() is external, its first statement is require(msg.sender == tx.origin), it then calls policy.rebase() and runs a list of downstream calls, and it reverts if one of them fails. The comment above it says contracts are guarded from calling to avoid flash loan attacks on liquidity providers. On chain at block 26472347 through the RPC in networks.json (reth v2.11.0): AMPL.monetaryPolicy() is 0x1b228a749077b8e307c5856ce62ef35d96dca2ea, policy.orchestrator() is the Orchestrator and Orchestrator.policy() points back, AMPL.balanceOf(PoolManager) is 16 base units, totalSupply is 1527834484102092 base units (9 decimals), inRebaseWindow() is 0, lastRebaseTimestampSec is 1795312800, the interval, offset and window length are 86400, 7200 and 1200 seconds, epoch is 2695 and the Orchestrator holds 4 downstream calls. eth_config reports fork id 0x07c9462e with activation time 1767747671. All of this matches the finding. The finding says it did not simulate a delegated account. I did, with eth_simulateV1 on the latest block (26472347 or a few blocks later) and a block time override of 1795399230, which lies inside the next rebase window. A call to rebase() from an account without code succeeded with 11 logs and 343,310 gas. The same call routed through a 51 byte forwarding contract placed by state override reverted after 24,029 gas with empty data, which is the origin check. An account whose code was overridden to the EIP-7702 designator 0xef0100 followed by the forwarder address then sent a transaction to itself. Its delegated code called rebase() and the call succeeded with the same 11 logs and 345,901 gas. Without the time override the plain account and the delegated account both reverted deeper in the call (43,028 and 45,618 gas) and the forwarder contract still stopped at 24,029 gas. A delegated account therefore passes the guard while it runs code, on the node that serves mainnet today. EIP-7702 (status Final) says in the section on self-sponsoring, lines 299 to 319, that the EIP breaks the invariant that msg.sender == tx.origin only happens in the topmost execution frame, and that the protection against atomic sandwich attacks such as flash loans would be broken. Lines 554 to 559 repeat this. The amount is zero today. In my simulated rebase the total supply and the PoolManager balance of 16 base units did not change. The last real rebase, at block 26467574, logged a supply change of 0 at a market rate of 1.2473 against a target of 1.2708. I reran the other triggers the finding names: Comptroller.claimComp(PoolManager) from an unrelated account succeeded and left the COMP balance at 5422.05, and Olympus staking rebase() succeeded and left the sOHM balance at 249.389779689, with epoch() reporting nothing to distribute. The Blockscout token list for the PoolManager had 66,563 rows at my fetch and shows the AMPL row with value 16. I found no primary source that contradicts the finding. I did not rerun the CometRewards claim and I did not read the source of the deployed monetary policy, which emits a newer rebase event than the policy code bundled with the Orchestrator source.
verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier. For a non-zero currency it reads balanceOf(PoolManager) and stores the currency and that value in transient storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). _settle reads the synced currency, rejects msg.value for a non-zero currency (line 356), computes paid as the current balance minus the stored value with checked subtraction (358-360), clears the synced currency (361) and credits the named recipient with paid (364). Nothing ties the rise to a transfer made by the settler. take debits msg.sender and then transfers (291-297). unlock calls unlockCallback on msg.sender and afterwards requires the count of open deltas to be zero (104-114). A credit of g from settle and a debit of g from take under the same currency and account cancel in _accountDelta (368-378), so the count check passes. I looked for a guard that would stop the sequence and found none. The msg.value check does not apply because no value is sent. The synced currency check in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52) only limits the fee controller. The int128 cast in settle and take (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59) limits an amount to 2^127 - 1, far above the AMPL supply. AMPL returns true from transfer, so the return data check in Currency.transfer passes (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). A search of the non-test sources shows that balanceOfSelf is called only at PoolManager.sol:285 and 359, so pool, position and claim accounting never see a rebase, and a positive one is credited to whoever brackets it. A negative rebase makes line 360 revert, so only gains can be booked. donate debits the donor and raises fee growth for in-range liquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:256-276, src/libraries/Pool.sol:466-480), so the mitigation described is available. sync is not the only route. take lets the caller hold the whole pooled AMPL balance for a nominal debit (291-297). If the rebase runs while the caller holds the tokens, the caller repays the nominal amount through sync, transfer and settle and keeps the growth. The result is the same as the bracket in the finding.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is right: every step is open to any account, and the pooled token and the pool are not made by the attacker. The assumptions should also list A5, because a take of the pooled balance before the rebase followed by a nominal repayment gives the same gain without a sync before the rebase. A change that only restricted sync would leave that route open. The supports text for the EIP source says the broken invariant is that msg.sender == tx.origin implies an account without code. The EIP words it as the check being true only in the topmost execution frame, and it says the use of the check to ensure that msg.sender is an EOA is unaffected. The conclusion for the Orchestrator guard is the same. The preconditions should say that recent rebases changed supply by zero (block 26467574, and my simulation of the next window), so a gain needs a market rate outside the policy's deviation band as well as a pool that holds AMPL. With 16 base units held, the gain rounds to zero today. The Blockscout row count was 66,563 at my fetch. Severity stays medium on the scale: the loss is limited to pools that hold an elastic supply or reward pushing token, and no such pool holds a material balance today.

findings.title: Polygon system token at 0x1010 mirrors the PoolManager native balance and cannot be paid out by take
findings.difference: Polygon has a genesis contract at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 that presents native POL as a token. Its balanceOf returns the native balance of the account. Its transfer is payable and returns false unless msg.value equals the amount. Ethereum has no ERC-20 face of ETH at the protocol level.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync(0x1010) stores balanceOf(PoolManager) as reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286, src/types/Currency.sol:94). That value is the full native POL balance of the PoolManager, which already backs pools that use address(0). 2. settle with 0x1010 synced credits the caller with any rise in that native balance since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). msg.value is rejected at src/PoolManager.sol:356 and the PoolManager has no receive function, so the balance can rise only through a forced transfer such as SELFDESTRUCT. 3. take(0x1010, to, amount) calls transfer on 0x1010 with zero value (src/types/Currency.sol:73). The token returns a 32 byte zero. The success test at src/types/Currency.sol:68 fails and the call reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. collectProtocolFees for this currency reverts the same way (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 4. A positive delta in currency 0x1010 can therefore only be cleared, minted as an ERC-6909 claim, or swapped. The POL that paid for it stays in the PoolManager native balance and no account holds a native delta to take it. 5. Double credit was checked and is not possible. A native settle while 0x1010 is synced reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:356, and sync(address(0)) clears the synced currency (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283), so one POL is never credited under both currencies.
findings.impact: POL that a contract pays into a pool or claim denominated in 0x1010 cannot leave the PoolManager as that currency and is not claimable as native POL either. Pools that hold POL under address(0) are not affected. The PoolManager held about 3.1 million native POL at the time of the query. Protocol fees accrued in currency 0x1010 would also be stuck.
findings.preconditions: Someone initializes a pool with 0x1010 as a currency, and a custom contract forces POL into the PoolManager between sync and settle. Standard periphery cannot do this because approve and transferFrom on 0x1010 revert. The actor loses its own funds. No path was found that takes funds from other users.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces, routers and pool indexers on Polygon should refuse 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 as a pool currency and direct users to address(0) or WPOL. Block explorers label 0x1010 as the POL token, so the warning should be explicit in deployment notes.

verification.factCheck: On chain at Polygon block 97,763,679 on 2026-11-22: eth_getBalance(PoolManager) and balanceOf(PoolManager) on 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 both return 0x294bb558a23f1f1a300e0, about 3,120,217 POL. symbol() returns POL. transfer(0xdead, 1) called from the PoolManager address with zero value returns a 32 byte zero. The same transfer with value 1 from a funded test address returns true, and with the PoolManager as recipient it reverts. A 1 wei call with empty calldata to the PoolManager reverts. approve and transferFrom revert. transferWithSig reverts with 'Disabled feature', so no signature path moves the PoolManager balance. The published MRC20.sol and BaseERC20NoSig.sol agree with these results: balanceOf returns account.balance, transfer returns false when msg.value differs from value, and _transfer uses address.transfer. The deployed code is 5315 bytes and contains the selectors of that source.
verification.codeCheck: sync(0x1010) stores the native balance as reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286, src/types/Currency.sol:94). _settle rejects msg.value while 0x1010 is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356) and credits balance minus reserves with a checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). settle and settleFor are the only payable functions (src/PoolManager.sol:300, src/PoolManager.sol:305) and the contract has no receive or fallback function, so only a forced transfer can raise the balance inside the window. take(0x1010) calls transfer with zero value (src/types/Currency.sol:73), receives a zero word, fails the test at src/types/Currency.sol:68 and reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. collectProtocolFees reverts the same way for this currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). I tried to turn the mirror into a double credit. A caller can take native POL, sync 0x1010, force the same POL back and receive a 0x1010 credit. The native debit from the take remains (src/PoolManager.sol:294). It can be cleared only with msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354) or by a swap against a pool that other users funded with 0x1010, and those users could fund it only by forcing in their own POL. Operations on a pool the caller funds alone conserve each currency, so the 0x1010 credit never becomes native credit for free. test/Sync.t.sol:255-274 covers the rejected native settle with the NativeERC20 model from src/test/NativeERC20.sol. No test covers a token whose transfer returns false for the PoolManager.
verification.corrections: Nothing wrong in the mechanism. One detail to add: a take of amount zero on 0x1010 would see transfer return true, and it changes nothing because a zero delta is ignored (src/PoolManager.sol:369). The frozen funds belong only to a party that chose to fund a 0x1010 position through a forced transfer, so low is the right level.

findings.title: Three more recipients on HyperEVM accept a PoolManager payout and strand it: the L1 block number precompile, the ERC-4337 EntryPoints and a system address reached through the stHYPE contract
findings.difference: HyperEVM has a precompile at 0x0809 that answers any call, with or without value, with the L1 block number. The ERC-4337 EntryPoints v0.6 and v0.7 are deployed and book incoming value as a deposit of the sender. HyperCore credits an ERC-20 sent to a token's system address only from the Transfer log of the linked contract, and for STHYPE the linked contract is wstHYPE, one of two contracts that move the same balance.
findings.mechanism: take debits the caller and then pays (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). Read-only calls from the PoolManager address show what three recipients do with the payout. A native payout of 1 wei to 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000809 returns success, so by the EVM's call rules the value is then held by a precompile address that cannot send it on (src/types/Currency.sol:44-53). A native payout to either EntryPoint succeeds and is booked as the PoolManager's deposit, which only the PoolManager could withdraw. Both EntryPoints answer balanceOf(PoolManager) with that deposit. A caller can therefore sync the EntryPoint address, make the payout and call settle, and is credited the same amount under the EntryPoint address as currency id (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365). That credit can be minted as an ERC-6909 claim and can never be paid out, because the EntryPoints revert on transfer(address,uint256). The caller still owes the native amount. A take of stHYPE to 0x2000000000000000000000000000000000000077 moves shares to the STHYPE system address while the linked contract, wstHYPE, emits no Transfer log, so by the documented rule HyperCore credits nobody. A take of wstHYPE to the same address is credited to the PoolManager's HyperCore account, as F-021 describes. In each case the caller pays the full amount and no other user loses anything.
findings.impact: The loss falls on the caller who chose the recipient, or on the user of a router that lets the user name any recipient. Pool reserves stay whole. Claims under an EntryPoint id are worthless and cannot affect another currency.
findings.preconditions: A caller or a router that passes one of these addresses as recipient. The stHYPE case needs stHYPE in the PoolManager, which holds none today, and the statement that HyperCore credits nothing rests on the docs and was not tested.
findings.mitigations: Routers and interfaces on HyperEVM should refuse recipients in 0x0800 to 0x08ff, the EntryPoint addresses, 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 and addresses that start with 0x20 followed by zeros, unless the payer chose them knowingly. The 0x settler contracts added a similar rule for HyperCore system addresses.

verification.factCheck: I reran the calls with the PoolManager as sender on 2026-11-22. 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000809 has no code and a zero balance, and it answers empty calldata with 1 wei of value, empty calldata without value, the transfer shape and the balanceOf shape with one 32 byte word that holds the L1 block number (0x495e7718 and following). A value call that succeeds leaves the value at that address. EntryPoint v0.7 (16,035 bytes) and v0.6 (23,689 bytes) both accept empty calldata with 1 wei from the PoolManager, answer balanceOf(PoolManager) with a 32 byte zero and revert on transfer(address,uint256). spotMeta lists STHYPE at index 119 with evmContract 0x94e8396e0869c9f2200760af0621afd240e1cf38, the wstHYPE contract, and the transfers page states that an EVM to HyperCore credit is taken from the Transfer log of the linked contract. In the verified source an stHYPE transfer emits Transfer from the stHYPE contract only (stHYPE.sol lines 244 to 256), while a wstHYPE transfer emits one log from each contract (wstHYPE.sol line 112 and stHYPE.sol line 285). The 0x settler changelog has the entry that payouts naming a HyperCore system address revert on HyperEVM unless the payer funds the transfer. That HyperCore credits nobody for an stHYPE transfer to 0x2000000000000000000000000000000000000077 follows from the documented rule and was not observed on chain.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller before the payout (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295). The native payout is a call with empty calldata and all gas whose only test is the success flag (src/types/Currency.sol:44-53), so a recipient that accepts value ends the matter for the PoolManager. For the EntryPoint id, sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286), settle credits the rise (lines 358-364), and a take under that id reverts because the EntryPoint reverts on transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). The credit therefore exists only as a delta or a claim under the EntryPoint address, and deltas and claims of one address cannot pay a debt under another (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16). The caller still owes the native amount when unlock checks the delta count (src/PoolManager.sol:112). I looked for a way to turn any of these into a gain at the cost of others and found none: anyone can raise the PoolManager's EntryPoint deposit through depositTo, and the result is the same worthless credit paid for in full.
verification.corrections: The stHYPE part is a consequence of the documented crediting rule and needs stHYPE in the PoolManager, which holds none. The actor value unprivileged is right in the sense that any caller can do it, and the loser is that caller or the user of a router that passes the recipient through. No other user loses funds.

findings.title: The OP Stack wrapped native predeploy on Celo calls itself Wrapped Ether and WETH but wraps CELO
findings.difference: On OP Stack chains that use ETH for gas, 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000006 is canonical WETH. On Celo the same address is a live wrapper of the native asset, which is CELO, and it still returns name 'Wrapped Ether' and symbol 'WETH' because the L2 L1Block predeploy reports the gas token as Ether. The bridged ETH token on Celo is a different contract at 0xD221812de1BD094f35587EE8E174B07B6167D9Af.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager accepts any address as a currency and reads no metadata (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). It learns balances only through balanceOf (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). Anyone can obtain the predeploy token one for one by depositing CELO. A pool, hook, router table or price source that treats this address as ETH backed WETH values a CELO backed token at the ETH price. Liquidity placed against it at that price is bought with tokens that cost one CELO each, and the paired asset leaves the PoolManager through ordinary swaps. Swappers who buy the token in such a pool receive a claim on CELO.
findings.impact: Funds of LPs and swappers in pools that list 0x4200...0006 as a currency, and integrations that map that address to WETH across OP Stack chains. Pools on the bridged WETH or on CELO are not affected. The PoolManager holds none of this token today, and its total supply is 0.143 CELO.
findings.preconditions: Someone must create or join a pool with the predeploy as a currency while pricing it as ETH, or an integration must hardcode the address as WETH. Any account can do the rest.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces and token lists for Celo should hide or relabel 0x4200...0006 and point to 0xD221...D9Af for ETH. Deployment scripts and routers should take the wrapped native address from Celo specific configuration. Pool creators should check that remoteToken() on a WETH candidate returns the Ethereum WETH address.

findings.title: Aave aTokens held by the Arbitrum One PoolManager grow outside pool accounting and the growth cannot be claimed
findings.difference: This is the rebasing token case that the Ethereum unit recorded for stETH, found here for Aave aTokens. No chain rule is involved. An aToken balance is a stored scaled amount multiplied by the reserve's liquidity index, so balanceOf(PoolManager) rises with time without any transfer.
findings.mechanism: Step 1: a liquidity provider adds liquidity in a pool whose currency is an aToken. The pool records a fixed amount and the PoolManager receives the aTokens. Step 2: the index grows with time and balanceOf(PoolManager) grows with it. For aArbUSDT the PoolManager has a scaled balance of 1,214.98 and a balance of 1,504.61. Step 3: a credit exists only for a balance increase between a sync and a settle in the same transaction (PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 358-360). The index does not move inside a transaction as far as I could establish: interest accrues with time and the Aave pool sends the whole flash loan premium to the protocol. I checked the premium setting on chain and did not read the Aave pool code for other paths. A sync therefore always includes the interest accrued so far in the reserve figure, and no settle is ever credited for it. Step 4: take, burn and fee collection pay out only recorded amounts, so the accrued interest stays in the PoolManager balance and belongs to no pool, claim or fee. The provider gets back the recorded amount and the pool fees. I found no way for an ordinary account to collect the surplus, and none to reduce the balance below the recorded amounts.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers in aToken pools lose the lending interest on their deposit for as long as it stays in the pool. Balances today are small: 1,504.6 aArbUSDT, 443.3 aArbUSDCn, 34.9 aArbUSDC and 0.41 aArbWETH. Principal is not affected.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use an aToken or another token whose balance rises without transfers. Nobody has to act. If a future Aave version again added value to the supplier index inside a transaction, an account that calls sync before it and settle after it would be credited the PoolManager's share of that addition.
findings.mitigations: Use a non-rebasing wrapper of the aToken as the pool currency. Interfaces can warn when a pool currency reports a scaled balance that differs from its balance.

sources.url: https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc eth_call scaledBalanceOf(PoolManager), balanceOf(PoolManager) and POOL() on aArbUSDT 0x6ab707Aca953eDAeFBc4fD23bA73294241490620 and aArbUSDCn 0x724dc807b04555b71ed48a6896b6F41593b8C637, and FLASHLOAN_PREMIUM_TOTAL() and FLASHLOAN_PREMIUM_TO_PROTOCOL() on 0x794a61358D6845594F94dc1DB02A252b5b4814aD, queried 2026-11-22
sources.supports: The PoolManager holds aTokens whose balance exceeds the scaled balance, and the Aave pool directs 100 percent of the flash loan premium to the protocol.
Yield is distributed to aToken holders by continuously increasing their balance, and balanceOf returns principal plus yield.
Aave v3.4 removed the part of the flash loan fee that was added to the supplier index, which leaves time based accrual as the only way the index rises.

verification.factCheck: I queried Arbitrum One on 2026-11-22. aArbUSDT 0x6ab707Aca953eDAeFBc4fD23bA73294241490620 returns balanceOf(PoolManager) 1,504.63 and scaledBalanceOf(PoolManager) 1,214.96, and aArbUSDCn 0x724dc807b04555b71ed48a6896b6F41593b8C637 returns 443.31 and 373.89. Both name 0x794a61358D6845594F94dc1DB02A252b5b4814aD as POOL(). That pool returns FLASHLOAN_PREMIUM_TOTAL() 5, FLASHLOAN_PREMIUM_TO_PROTOCOL() 10000 and POOL_REVISION() 12, and it reverts with empty data on backUnbacked and mintUnbacked, so the bridge path that once added to the supplier index is not present. The Aave v3.4 proposal says the part of the flash loan fee that went to suppliers was removed and that yield accrual becomes the only entry point for a liquidity index increase. The Aave documentation says yield is distributed by continuously increasing the holder's balance. I did not read the Aave pool source at revision 12, so the statement that no call inside one transaction raises the index rests on the proposal text and the two on-chain settings.
verification.codeCheck: sync records balanceOf(PoolManager) at the moment of the call (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286) and _settle credits reservesNow minus that record (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). Transient storage does not outlive the transaction, so the record and the settle always fall in one transaction and one block timestamp. A balance that grows only with time is therefore fully inside the record and never produces a credit. I looked for any other path that pays out balance above the recorded amounts and found none: take debits the caller the full amount (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295), burn needs existing claims (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336), collectProtocolFees is limited to protocolFeesAccrued (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56), and a sync of address zero only clears the currency slot (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-25). The accrued interest stays in the PoolManager balance and belongs to no pool, claim or caller.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is acceptable only in the sense that no privilege is needed. No account acts and no account gains. Nothing is taken from the PoolManager and nothing is frozen, so this item is outside the goal of the review and should be reported as lost yield for providers who choose a rebasing currency. The scaled balance of aArbUSDT read 1,214.96 at my query against 1,214.98 in the finding. The warning in the preconditions is the part worth keeping: a token whose balanceOf(PoolManager) can be raised by a call that any account may make inside a transaction would let that account collect the PoolManager's share through sync and settle. Lead 5 of the research file covers the search for such a token and I add what I found on xUSD as a lead.

findings.title: Any account can fill a boundary tick to the per tick liquidity cap for a dust payment, which blocks later deposits that use that tick
findings.difference: None. The cap and the amount formula are part of the pool math and give the same numbers on every network. Read-only probes against the PoolManager on 20 of the 21 networks returned identical results. Tempo could not be probed with a native payment because the node rejects calls that carry value.
findings.mechanism: Pool.modifyLiquidity adds liquidityDelta to liquidityGross of the lower and the upper tick of the range (src/libraries/Pool.sol:160-162, 524-531). For a delta of zero or more it reverts with TickLiquidityOverflow when liquidityGross of either tick is above tickSpacingToMaxLiquidityPerTick (Pool.sol:165-173). The cap is (2^128 - 1) divided by the number of ticks (Pool.sol:565-582): 191757530477355301479181766273477 for spacing 1, 1917559095893846719543856547154045 for spacing 10, 11505354575363080317263139282924270 for spacing 60 and 38345995821606768476828330790147420 for spacing 200, which are the values in test/Tick.t.sol:115-141. A range that lies above the current tick is paid in currency0 only, with getAmount0Delta(sqrtLower, sqrtUpper, liquidity) rounded up (Pool.sol:209-217, src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:188-211, 261-271). That amount is liquidity times the difference of the inverse sqrt prices, and at the highest usable ticks the sqrt prices are close to 2^160, so the amount is tiny. Filling the highest usable tick to the cap with a range one spacing wide costs 519,766,372 base units of currency0 at spacing 1, 51,993,092,462 at spacing 10, 1,878,783,905,959 at spacing 60 and 20,966,766,746,469 at spacing 200. The mirror case at the lowest usable tick is paid in currency1 and costs 519,766,206, 51,993,074,932, 1,878,783,895,257 and 20,966,766,629,403 base units. The cost does not depend on where the pool trades as long as the range is out of range. After the fill, every add whose range starts or ends on that tick reverts, whoever the owner is and however small the amount. An owner who removes liquidity from that tick can add back at most what it removed. Removals never run the cap check, because the check sits inside the branch for a delta of zero or more (Pool.sol:165), so nothing is locked. The filler can remove its position at any time and gets its payment back, so the fill costs gas and idle dust. Flash accounting does not make it free: the position has to stay, so the debit has to be settled. I confirmed the numbers three ways. A Python transcription of Pool, Position, TickBitmap, SqrtPriceMath and TickMath gives them. An eth_call through the PositionManager on Ethereum for the ETH/USDC 0.05 percent pool (spacing 10) minted 1917559095893846714755826590044058 units of liquidity on the range 887260 to 887270 with a value of 51,993,092,462 wei, reverted with one wei less, and reverted with TickLiquidityOverflow(887270) for one more unit of liquidity. The same three calls on a pool created inside the call gave the same outcome on 20 networks for spacings 1, 60 and 200.
findings.impact: New deposits that use the filled tick stop in that pool. This covers the usual full range position and every position that ends on the lowest or highest usable tick. Principal and fees of existing positions are not touched and can be withdrawn. A liquidity provider can avoid the block by choosing an outer tick further inside, at the price of a position that front ends do not show as full range. A contract that always adds on the filled tick, such as a full range vault or a hook that holds one fixed full range position, cannot take deposits or reinvest fees while the fill stands. If such a contract has to add liquidity on that tick before it can pay out, its withdrawals stop too. I looked for one deployed contract of that kind and did not find it, so the freeze variant is unconfirmed. For a currency with 18 decimals the cost is below 0.00003 of one token for every spacing up to 200. For a currency with 6 decimals it is about 520 tokens at spacing 1 and about 1.88 million tokens at spacing 60, so the attacker fills the end whose currency is cheap per base unit. On the Ethereum ETH/USDC 0.05 percent pool the liquidityGross of tick 887270 was 4788029957109987 at block 26471794, 18 orders of magnitude under the cap, and the fill costs about 0.00000005 ETH.
findings.preconditions: An initialized pool in which at least one of the two currencies is cheap per base unit. Any account can act. No hook, no role and no ordering advantage is needed. The fill lasts until the filler removes its position.
findings.mitigations: Core has no switch for this. Front ends and liquidity providers can fall back to an outer tick one or more spacings inside the usable range when the boundary tick is full. Authors of vaults and hooks should not hard-code the lowest and highest usable ticks in any path that must succeed for a withdrawal, and should let the range be changed. Operators can watch liquidityGross of the two boundary ticks of important pools through extsload and compare it with the cap.

sources.supports: The cap is checked only when liquidityDelta is zero or more, on liquidityGross of both ticks.
A range above the current tick is paid in currency0 only, from the sqrt prices of its two ticks.

findings.title: The swap loop pays for every bitmap word and every initialized tick on its way, and a HyperEVM small block holds 3,000,000 gas
findings.difference: HyperEVM produces small blocks with a 3,000,000 gas limit every second and big blocks with a 30,000,000 gas limit about once a minute. A sender reaches big blocks only after setting the usingBigBlocks flag on its HyperCore account. I sampled blocks 51958402 to 51958471 through the public RPC: 69 had gasLimit 3,000,000 and one (51958443) had 30,000,000. For comparison, state/networks.json records an Ethereum block gas limit of 59,999,943, and EIP-7825 specifies a cap of 16,777,216 gas per transaction. I did not confirm in this session that the cap is active on Ethereum.
findings.mechanism: Pool.swap runs one loop iteration per step (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437). Each iteration reads one tick bitmap word from storage (Pool.sol:347-348, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:85-121), computes the price of the next tick and runs one swap step. When the step ends on an initialized tick, crossTick reads the tick slot and reads and rewrites both fee growth slots of that tick (Pool.sol:413-428, 602-612). The repository gas snapshots give 2,242 to 2,287 gas for the bitmap search, which includes the cold storage read, and 919 to 1,565 gas for a swap step with liquidity. I use 2,242 gas as the floor for one iteration and leave out the swap step, TickMath and loop bookkeeping. A crossing adds one cold read (2,100) and two read and write pairs. Each pair costs 5,000 gas when the slot changes from one nonzero value to another and 22,100 gas when it is written for the first time. That gives about 14,342 gas per crossing when both fee growth slots change, and about 48,542 when both are written for the first time. With the repository figure of 123,144 gas for a simple swap as fixed cost, a 3,000,000 gas transaction fits at most about 200 crossings, about 59 when the fee growth slots are written for the first time, and about 1,283 empty bitmap words. The real numbers are lower, because the floor leaves out the computation. I did not measure gas on HyperEVM. Three things an ordinary account controls raise the iteration count of other people's swaps. First, modifyLiquidity lets anyone add a position of one liquidity unit on any aligned tick pair of a pool without a hook (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184, Pool.sol:159-181). In my transcription of the source, 200 such positions on [t, t+1) below the price of a pool with tick spacing 1 made every tick initialized, each cost 1 base unit of one currency, and a swap that moved the price by 100, 200 and 400 ticks ran 101, 201 and 401 iterations, each with a crossing. Second, a step with zero liquidity in range consumes nothing and moves the price to the next word boundary (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-75), so a swap that runs past the last position toward its price limit visits every word on the way. From tick 0 to the lower limit that is 3,468 iterations at tick spacing 1, 349 at spacing 10, 60 at spacing 60 and 20 at spacing 200, which is at least 7,775,256 gas at spacing 1 from the bitmap reads alone. Third, initialize has no access control and accepts any price from MIN_SQRT_PRICE up to one unit below MAX_SQRT_PRICE (PoolManager.sol:117-142, Pool.sol:100-107), so a third party can create a pool id at an extreme price before anyone else uses it. The gap to the market price then has to be walked with swaps that take no tokens and still pay for every word.
findings.impact: No funds leave the PoolManager and no position is frozen. Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop (Pool.sol:146-238), so removals fit in a small block in every case I looked at. The cost falls on swappers and arbitrageurs in pools with tick spacing 1 or other small spacings. In a pool where every tick carries a dust position, one small block transaction can move the price by at most about 59 to 200 ticks, which is 0.6 to 2.0 percent at spacing 1. A larger move needs several transactions with nearer price limits, or a big block. A swap that names the extreme price limit and exceeds the liquidity on its side runs out of gas in a small block where it would otherwise end with a partial fill. A contract that must complete one large swap in one transaction, for example a liquidation, can stall until it is sent to a big block. The dust positions cost the attacker about 161,276 gas each by the repository snapshot for a simple add, plus one base unit, and stay until the attacker removes them.
findings.preconditions: The pool has a small tick spacing, since at spacing 60 a move of 59 crossings is already more than 40 percent. The attacker pays gas for each dust position. The victim sends the swap to a small block, or the swap sits inside a contract that cannot split it. Any account can undo the third case by walking the price in several transactions.
findings.mitigations: Routers and keepers on HyperEVM can pass a price limit close to the expected end price and split large swaps. Contracts that depend on one atomic swap can use pools with a wider tick spacing or send the transaction to a big block. Pool creators can initialize the pool ids they intend to use at the market price before announcing them. Liquidity providers do not need to act, because removal does not loop.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the Hyperliquid page on the dual block architecture. It states a fast block duration of 1 second with a 3M gas limit and a slow block duration of 1 minute with a 30M gas limit, and that a sender is moved to big blocks by the HyperCore action evmUserModify with usingBigBlocks true. I queried eth_getBlockByNumber on https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm for blocks 51958402 to 51958471 myself: 69 blocks report gasLimit 3,000,000 and block 51958443 reports 30,000,000, as the finding says. The largest gasUsed in the sample was 1,860,095. The HyperEVM page states that the chain uses the Cancun hardfork without blobs. I tested the gas schedule for storage reads instead of inferring it: eth_estimateGas for PoolManager.extsload(startSlot, nSlots) with 1, 2, 51 and 101 empty slots returned 24,293, 26,473, 133,821 and 244,561 on HyperEVM and the same four numbers on Ethereum, which is about 2,200 gas per extra cold slot on both. The cold read cost of 2,100 that the estimate rests on therefore holds on HyperEVM. I fetched EIP-2929 (COLD_SLOAD_COST, SSTORE_RESET_GAS equal to 5000 minus COLD_SLOAD_COST), EIP-2200 (SSTORE_SET_GAS 20000, SSTORE_RESET_GAS 5000) and EIP-3529 (refund cap of one fifth of gas used). I did not measure SSTORE cost on HyperEVM, so the write costs rest on the Cancun statement in the docs. I fetched EIP-7825 and EIP-7607: the 16,777,216 gas cap per transaction is part of Fusaka, which activated on Ethereum mainnet on 2025-12-03, so the comparison value is in force. The repository snapshots hold the numbers the finding quotes (snapshots/TickBitmapTest.json:5-10, snapshots/SwapMathTest.json:2-9, snapshots/PoolManagerTest.json:12 and 16). I found no primary source that contradicts the finding. Not confirmed: the gas of one loop iteration of the deployed bytecode on HyperEVM was not measured by the researcher or by me. verification.codeCheck: I read the swap path and wrote my own transcription of BitMath, FullMath, TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap and Pool from the source text. Pool.swap runs one loop pass per call to nextInitializedTickWithinOneWord (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-348), and that call reads one bitmap word from storage (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:98 and 111). A pass that ends on an initialized tick calls crossTick, which reads and rewrites feeGrowthOutside0X128 and feeGrowthOutside1X128 and reads the slot that holds liquidityNet (Pool.sol:413-428, 602-612). No guard bounds the number of passes other than the amount and the price limit (Pool.sol:344). With liquidity 0 a step consumes nothing and ends on its target (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-75), so a swap toward a far limit visits every word. modifyLiquidity has no access check for a pool without a hook (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184) and Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop (Pool.sol:146-238), so removals are not affected. initialize accepts any price that getTickAtSqrtPrice accepts (PoolManager.sol:117-142, Pool.sol:100-107, src/libraries/TickMath.sol:121-129). In my transcription 200 positions of liquidity 1 on [t, t+1) for t from -200 to -1 in a spacing 1 pool cost 200 base units of currency1 in total, and a swap that moved the price by 100 and 200 ticks ran 101 and 201 passes. An empty pool walked from tick 0 to the lower limit ran 3,467 passes at spacing 1, 348 at spacing 10, 59 at spacing 60 and 19 at spacing 200, and returned the delta (0, 0). The arithmetic of the bounds is right: (3,000,000 - 123,144) / 14,342 is 200, / 48,542 is 59 and / 2,242 is 1,283. At 2,100 gas per cold read alone the spacing 1 walk needs more than 7,280,000 gas, which is above a small block. Actor check: every step is open to an ordinary account, the affected pools need no hook and no attacker token, and the victims only swap. The actor value unprivileged is right. Severity check: no funds leave and no position is locked, a swap can be split or sent to a big block, so low is right and the effect degrade is right.
verification.corrections: The finding says it did not confirm that the EIP-7825 cap is active on Ethereum. It is active since Fusaka on 2025-12-03. The run with 200 dust positions cannot give 401 passes for a 400 tick move: my transcription gives 203 passes (201 crossings of the ticks from 0 down to -200 and two further passes to the word end and to the limit), and 401 passes need about 400 dusted ticks. My pass counts for the empty walk are one lower than the finding's (3,467, 348, 59 and 19), which changes the bitmap floor to 7,773,014 gas and changes no conclusion. The 48,542 gas case needs both fee growth outside slots of a tick to go from zero to nonzero. That happens for a tick above the current price when it is crossed upward for the first time while both global fee growth values are nonzero (Pool.sol:533-539, 608-609). Dust placed below the price starts with both slots equal to the global values, so those crossings fall in the 14,342 gas case or lower. The attacker can bring a tick back to the first time state by removing and adding the dust position again. Refunds for slots set to zero are paid after execution and do not lower the gas limit a swap needs. The evidence grade can move from inferred to primary for the block limits and the cold read cost. The per pass total on HyperEVM stays an upper bound on the number of crossings until someone measures it.

findings.title: One transaction can use the whole per-block budget for new state on MegaETH, and the node skips every later candidate of that block
findings.difference: MegaETH counts new accounts and new storage slots per transaction and per block, and both limits are 1,000 entries. Ethereum has no such counter. The block limiter admits the transaction that brings the block counter to the limit and then rejects every further candidate before execution, whatever that candidate would do. The base fee has stayed at its floor of 1,000,000 wei in every block sampled.
findings.mechanism: A sender submits one transaction that creates 1,000 new state entries, for example a contract creation that writes 999 fresh storage slots. eth_estimateGas accepts that creation at 22,559,525 gas, which at the base fee of 1,000,000 wei is about 0.0000226 ETH, and rejects a creation with 1,000 slots. Storage gas is zero for slots in buckets of minimum size, so the cost is the compute gas of the writes. After this transaction the block counter for state growth equals the block limit. BlockLimiter::pre_execution_check then returns StateGrowthLimit for every later candidate of that block, including a liquidity removal or a take that creates no new state. Those candidates are skipped and can enter a later block. A sender who repeats this in every one second block spends about 1.95 ETH per day. Calls to modifyLiquidity and take on the PoolManager have no path that avoids the block limiter. What the sender achieves depends on where its transaction lands inside each block. Candidates placed before it are included. The ordering rule of the sequencer was not confirmed, so the share of each block that the sender can close was not established.
findings.impact: Removals, swaps and claims on the PoolManager can be delayed block by block while the sender keeps paying. No balance moves and no position changes. The delay ends when the sender stops or when users' transactions are ordered ahead of the sender's.
findings.preconditions: The base fee stays near its floor, and the sender's transaction is ordered early in each block. No role is needed. A full stop of withdrawals would need the sender to be first in every block, which the public record does not show to be possible.
findings.mitigations: Core has no setting for this. Users can resubmit, pay a higher priority fee if the sequencer orders by fee, or use the L1 deposit path, whose transactions are placed at the start of a block in the OP Stack design. That placement was not confirmed in the MegaETH node source. The chain operator can raise the block limit above the transaction limit or price new state entries in minimum-size buckets.

BlockLimiter::pre_execution_check returns MegaBlockLimitExceededError::StateGrowthLimit for a candidate when block_state_growth_used is at or above the limit (lines 880 to 890), and the is_deposit flag gates only the two data availability tests (lines 821 to 845). post_execution_update_raw adds the usage of an executed transaction without a test, and its comment says the last transaction is allowed to exceed the limit (lines 895 to 943). The specification page states that the first transaction that brings the block to the limit must be included and that later candidates must be skipped before execution. The Rex upgrade page lists state growth of 1,000 per transaction and per block as a new limit. gas.rs computes the storage gas of a new slot as 20,000 times (multiplier minus 1), which is zero at multiplier 1 (lines 49 to 51). On chain, eth_estimateGas for a contract creation that writes n new slots returned 120,922 gas for n = 1, 22,559,391 gas for n = 999 and 'execution reverted' for n = 1,000 and n = 1,001, so the transaction limit of 1,000 entries with the new account counted as one is live on mainnet. The latest block and blocks 10,000,000, 20,000,000, 25,000,000, 30,000,000 and 32,000,000 report a base fee of 1,000,000 wei, and eth_feeHistory over the last 100 blocks shows the same base fee and a median priority fee of zero. At that price 22.56 million gas is 0.0000226 ETH, and 86,400 such transactions cost about 1.95 ETH. I found no primary source that contradicts the finding. Two links stay unconfirmed. I did not observe a mainnet block that was closed in this way, so the behaviour of the live sequencer rests on the reference implementation and the specification. The ordering rule of the sequencer is not documented in the pages I read. A podcast transcript with the MegaETH founders says the team rejects tip auctions per block, which is a secondary source.
verification.codeCheck: The finding needs nothing from the PoolManager code beyond the fact that its calls are ordinary transactions. modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184) and take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) require the unlocked flag, which exists only inside a call to unlock made in the same transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, src/libraries/Lock.sol:11-27). No function in src/ reads a block field or offers a path that a third party could execute for a user after a delay, so a withdrawal that is skipped for one block has to be included in a later block as a whole transaction. No state of a pool changes while the transaction waits, apart from what other included transactions do to the pool price. I found no guard in src/ that bears on this, and none is possible at contract level.
verification.corrections: The gas figure differs slightly with my own init code (22,559,391 against 22,559,525), which does not change the cost. The specification says later candidates are skipped when they depend on the exhausted resource, while the reference limiter skips every candidate. The finding follows the limiter, and that is the stricter reading. The precondition is stated too narrowly. The finding says a full stop needs the sender to be first in every block. If the sequencer serves pending transactions in arrival order, a run of N such transactions submitted together from several accounts would close N consecutive blocks for every transaction that arrives after the run, at 0.0000226 ETH per block. If the sequencer orders by priority fee, the same run with a priority fee of 1 wei outranks the current traffic, whose median priority fee is zero, until users pay more. This extension follows from the limiter logic and was not observed on chain. The severity stays low for the confirmed part, which is a delay inside one block. It would be medium under the scale if the multi-block case is confirmed, because liquidity operations would be blocked without loss for as long as the sender pays. The operator of the single sequencer can exclude such transactions, so the stall would last until the operator reacts.

findings.title: A HyperCore transfer makes the node call a linked contract with 200,000 gas ahead of every signed transaction in the block
findings.difference: HyperCore credits a spot transfer to the EVM through a system transaction that calls transfer(recipient, amount) on the contract linked to the token, with the token's system address as sender, gas price 0 and 200,000 gas. The docs state that the linked contract may have arbitrary bytecode and give no guarantee about what its transfer function does. Deploying and linking a spot token is open to anyone; the deploy auction stood at 500 on 2026-11-22. System transactions are placed before all signed transactions of the block and their gas does not count toward the block gas limit. On Ethereum only the block builder decides which code runs first.
findings.mechanism: An account deploys a spot token on HyperCore, links it to a contract it wrote and sends the token to the token's system address. The node then calls that contract's transfer function at the top of an EVM block, before any signed transaction. Inside the call the contract is an ordinary caller of the PoolManager. It can call unlock, which calls unlockCallback on it (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), swap, and settle with tokens or ERC-6909 claims it holds (src/PoolManager.sol:187-227 and 322-336). The PoolManager gives the system address and the linked contract no role, and transient state is cleared after the system transaction like after any other, so nothing carries into the signed transactions. What the account gains is position: it reaches every pool before transactions that paid a priority fee, for the price of one HyperCore action. That is the first leg of a sandwich, or first place for arbitrage after a price move. A swapper loses at most what the price limit and slippage setting of the swap allow. Reserves, positions and claims of other users are not reachable this way.
findings.impact: Swappers in any pool can be traded against from the first position of a block by an account without validator rights. The loss per swap is bounded by the swapper's own limits. LP principal and claims are unaffected.
findings.preconditions: The attacker deploys and links one spot token. The pool action must fit in 200,000 gas; I did not measure a complete swap against that limit. I did not confirm how HyperCore orders several system transactions inside one block, which EVM block follows a given HyperCore action, or whether pending EVM transactions are visible to the attacker in time.
findings.mitigations: Swappers and routers should set tight price limits. Routers should not treat a quote from one block as valid at the top of the next. Pools that need protection from first position trading have to add it in a hook.

verification.factCheck: The Hyperliquid transfers page states that a HyperCore to HyperEVM transfer is credited by a system transaction that calls transfer(recipient, amount) on the linked contract as the system address, that it costs 200k gas at the base gas price of the next HyperEVM block, that the linked contract may have arbitrary bytecode and that nothing is guaranteed about what the transfer call does. In the archive client, src/node/types/mod.rs lines 83 to 101 split a block body into the first system_tx_count transactions and the rest, src/node/evm/executor.rs lines 225 to 227 add gas to the block total only when is_system_transaction is false, and lines 39 to 43 define a system transaction as one with gas price zero. On chain I read eth_getSystemTxsByBlockNumber for 40 blocks ending at 51,966,640. Four system transactions came from 0x2000000000000000000000000000000000000157 and called transfer on the linked contract 0x33af3c2540ba72054e044efe504867b39ae421f5 with 200,000 gas and gas price 0. In block 51,966,623, which holds two system transactions, the first signed transaction has cumulativeGasUsed equal to its own gasUsed (325,780), so the system transactions are not counted. The public RPC returns no receipt for a system transaction hash, so the statement that they execute before the signed transactions rests on the block layout in the archive client and its README. spotDeployState returns a gas auction with startGas 500.0, endGas 500.0 and currentGas null; the finding quotes currentGas 500.0. The dual block page states that the HyperEVM mempool is onchain state of the L1, which is relevant to whether pending transactions can be seen. I found no source that contradicts the finding.
verification.codeCheck: unlock is open to any caller and calls unlockCallback on msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). swap, modifyLiquidity, take, settle, mint and burn check only the unlock flag (src/PoolManager.sol:96-99, 187-227, 291-336). No line in src outside src/test reads tx.origin or compares msg.sender with a fixed address other than the hook self call test (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175) and the owner and controller tests (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29 and 36 and 48). A linked contract that runs inside a system transaction is therefore an ordinary caller. It must leave every delta at zero before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112), so it pays for what it takes. The pinned revm fork clears transient storage in commit_tx, so the unlock flag, deltas and synced currency do not carry into the first signed transaction. The effect is position in the block and nothing else: reserves, positions and claims of other users are not reachable through this path.
verification.corrections: The finding's own open points stay open: I did not measure whether an unlock with a swap and settlement in claims fits in 200,000 gas, and I did not confirm the order of several system transactions or how early a HyperCore action must be sent to land ahead of a given signed transaction. One addition: the exchange API documents a sendToEvmWithData action that calls coreReceiveWithData on the linked contract with a gasLimit and a data field chosen by the sender, so the 200,000 gas figure may not bound what a linked contract can do at the top of a block. The auction field that reads 500.0 is startGas and endGas. This is an ordering hazard for swappers within their own price limits and is no path to funds held for other users.

findings.title: A native payout sent to a withdrawal predeploy, a fee vault, an EntryPoint or a Celo core contract is lost to the caller on Celo and X Layer
findings.difference: Both chains have contracts that accept a plain native transfer and book it to msg.sender or keep it. On Celo these are L2ToL1MessagePasser (0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000016), the fee vaults at 0x11, 0x19, 0x1a and 0x1b, the L1BlockNumber predeploy at 0x13, the wrapped native predeploy at 0x06, the three ERC-4337 EntryPoints, and the Celo core contracts FeeHandler, MentoFeeHandlerSeller, UniswapFeeHandlerSeller, Reserve and Governance. On X Layer the fee vaults, 0x13, both Wrapped OKB contracts and the EntryPoints accept value. The X Layer L2ToL1MessagePasser refuses value because the chain runs in custom gas token mode.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(address(0), to, amount) debits the caller by amount and makes the PoolManager send amount of the native asset to the recipient with empty calldata (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:44-52). The recipient sees the PoolManager as msg.sender. 2. On Celo, L2ToL1MessagePasser.receive() calls initiateWithdrawal(msg.sender, 100000, empty data). The CELO leaves the L2 and the withdrawal names the PoolManager address as L1 target. That address has no code and no balance on Ethereum. 3. An EntryPoint books the amount as a deposit of the PoolManager. The PoolManager cannot call withdrawTo, and the EntryPoint spends a deposit only after the account answers a validation call that src/ does not implement. 4. A fee vault, the Reserve, the FeeHandler contracts and Governance keep the amount as their own balance. 5. The wrapped native contracts mint wrapped tokens to the PoolManager address. A caller who syncs the wrapper first and settles afterwards is credited that amount under the wrapper's currency id, which is an ordinary wrap at one to one. 6. In every case the caller still owes amount in currency address(0) and must pay it before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 349-364). Pool reserves are unchanged in total. 7. A caller who syncs an EntryPoint, takes native value to it and settles is credited amount under the EntryPoint's currency id, because the EntryPoint's balanceOf is the deposit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-360). The EntryPoint has no transfer function, so that credit can never be taken (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86).
findings.impact: The loss is the amount of one payout and falls on the account that chose the recipient. No pool reserve, no claim of another user and no protocol fee is reduced, and an attacker gains nothing by doing this on purpose.
findings.preconditions: A user, a router or a front end passes one of these addresses as the recipient of a native take. Core gives no third party a way to choose the recipient of another account's payout. Whether the deployed routers and the PositionManager filter recipients was not read.
findings.mitigations: Routers and front ends can refuse the predeploy range, the EntryPoint addresses and the Celo core contract addresses as recipients of native payouts. Users who want CELO on Ethereum should take to their own account and withdraw from there.

The debit stays open until the caller settles, because unlock reverts while any delta is nonzero (src/PoolManager.sol:112). For the EntryPoint case, sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) of any address (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) and the settle path credits the rise under that address as currency (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). The credit cannot be taken, because the ERC-20 branch of transfer reverts when the call fails (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). The caller must clear it or mint it as a claim to close the unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329). Pool reserves and other users' claims are untouched in every variant.
verification.corrections: No change to actor or severity. The actor value unprivileged is acceptable only in the sense that no role is needed. The one party that loses is the account that named the recipient, so this item is no path to other users' funds and no attacker gains from it. Step 7 should add that the credit under the EntryPoint id has to be cleared or minted before unlock returns. The op-stack-eth unit recorded the same hazard for the ETH chains, and the two entries can be merged.

findings.title: A native payout sent to L2ToL1MessagePasser, an ERC-4337 EntryPoint or the L1BlockNumber predeploy is booked to the PoolManager's own address and is lost to the caller
findings.difference: OP Stack chains have a withdrawal contract, L2ToL1MessagePasser at 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000016, whose receive() starts a withdrawal to L1 for msg.sender and uses msg.sender as the L1 target. Ethereum has no contract with that behaviour. The legacy L1BlockNumber predeploy at 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000013 accepts ETH with any calldata and has no function that pays it out. The ERC-4337 EntryPoint, which also exists on Ethereum, credits a plain ETH transfer as a deposit of msg.sender.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(address(0), to, amount) debits the caller by amount and then makes the PoolManager send amount of ETH to the recipient with empty calldata and all gas (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:44-52). The recipient sees the PoolManager as msg.sender. 2. If the recipient is L2ToL1MessagePasser, its receive() calls initiateWithdrawal(msg.sender, 100000, empty data). The ETH is taken off the L2 and a withdrawal is recorded with the PoolManager as sender and the PoolManager's address as the L1 target. The PoolManager addresses of all seven chains have no code on Ethereum. If the withdrawal is proven and finalised on L1, the ETH is delivered to that address, where nothing can move it. The value call returned success in eth_call on OP Mainnet, Base and Unichain. 3. If the recipient is an EntryPoint, receive() calls depositTo(msg.sender) and the amount becomes a deposit of the PoolManager. withdrawTo pays out only the deposit of its own caller, and the PoolManager cannot call it. The EntryPoint spends a deposit only after the account answers validateUserOp or validatePaymasterUserOp, and src/ has neither function, so the deposit cannot be spent. 4. If the recipient is L1BlockNumber, the fallback keeps the ETH and returns the L1 block number. 5. In each case the caller still owes amount in currency address(0) and must pay it with msg.value before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 349-364). Pool reserves are unchanged in total: amount left and amount came back in. The caller has paid for a payout that reached nobody. 6. A caller who first calls sync(EntryPoint), then takes native ETH to the EntryPoint and then calls settle is credited amount under the currency id of the EntryPoint, because balanceOf(PoolManager) on the EntryPoint is the deposit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-360). That credit can be minted as an ERC-6909 claim and can never be paid out, because the EntryPoint has no transfer function and take reverts (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). The native debt from step 1 remains and must still be paid in full.
findings.impact: The loss is the amount of one payout and falls on the account that chose the recipient. No pool reserve, no other user's claim and no protocol fee is reduced, and an attacker gains nothing by doing this on purpose. One sign that the L1 twin addresses do receive stray value: the Base PoolManager address holds 0.0588 ETH and no code on Ethereum. How that ETH arrived was not traced.
findings.preconditions: A user, a router or a front end passes one of these addresses as the recipient of a native take, for example in the belief that sending ETH to the message passer bridges it to the user's own L1 address. No third party can choose the recipient of someone else's payout through core. Whether the deployed Universal Router or PositionManager filter recipients was not read.
findings.mitigations: Routers and front ends can refuse the predeploy range 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 0x42000000000000000000000000000000000007ff and the EntryPoint addresses as recipients of native payouts. Users who want ETH on L1 should take to their own account and withdraw from there. Nothing in core can be configured to prevent it.
