verification.factCheck: I fetched the four cited contract sources and reran the chain queries on 22 November 2026. L2ToL1MessagePasser.sol on the develop branch has RECEIVE_DEFAULT_GAS_LIMIT = 100000 at line 21 and a receive function at lines 60-62 that calls initiateWithdrawal(msg.sender, RECEIVE_DEFAULT_GAS_LIMIT, bytes('')). initiateWithdrawal records msg.sender as sender and the first argument as target, so a payout from the PoolManager names the PoolManager address as the L1 target. StakeManager.sol at tag v0.7.0 has receive() calling depositTo(msg.sender) at lines 42-44, balanceOf returning deposits[account].deposit at lines 38-40 and withdrawTo debiting deposits[msg.sender] at lines 134-146. EntryPoint.sol at v0.7.0 lowers a sender deposit at line 504 after the validateUserOp call at line 490 and a paymaster deposit at line 535 before the validatePaymasterUserOp call at line 538, and a revert of either call ends in FailedOpWithRevert (lines 496 and 547), which undoes the debit. L1BlockNumber.sol has payable receive and fallback functions that return the L1 block number as one word and no other state changing function. On chain I used eth_call with the PoolManager code overridden by a forwarding stub, so the target saw the PoolManager as msg.sender and a separate tx.origin. On all seven chains a 0.001 ETH call with empty calldata succeeds at L2ToL1MessagePasser, at EntryPoint v0.6, v0.7 and v0.8, at L1BlockNumber and at the fee vaults, and reverts at L2StandardBridge with 'StandardBridge: function can only be called from an EOA'. On OP Mainnet and Base a Multicall3 call showed the effect: balanceOf(PoolManager) at each of the three EntryPoints went from 0 to 1000000000000000 after the value call, and messageNonce() of the message passer rose by one (0x8b67 to 0x8b68 on OP Mainnet, 0x209c2 to 0x209c3 on Base). transfer(address,uint256) from the PoolManager reverts at all three EntryPoints on all seven chains, and L1BlockNumber answers transfer and balanceOf with the L1 block number (0x193eea2 at the time), which is never 1. On Ethereum, eth_getCode is empty and the nonce is 0 at all seven PoolManager addresses, and eth_getBalance at 0x498581ff718922c3f8e6a244956af099b2652b2b is 58773641109313318 wei. I found no primary source that contradicts the finding. I did not read the EntryPoint v0.6 and v0.8 sources and rely on the eth_call results for those two versions.
verification.codeCheck: take requires only the unlocked flag, debits msg.sender by amount and then transfers (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For currency address(0) the transfer is call(gas(), to, amount, 0, 0, 0, 0) and reverts only if that call fails (src/types/Currency.sol:45-53). Nothing in that path looks at the recipient, so a recipient that accepts the value and books it to msg.sender leaves the PoolManager as the owner of the deposit or withdrawal. The debit is a negative delta of the caller under address(0). unlock reverts while any delta is open (src/PoolManager.sol:112), and a native debt can be closed only by settle with msg.value while the synced currency is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354, 364), by burning address(0) claims (332-336) or by a pool credit, so the caller pays the full amount. Step 6 also holds. sync has no lock check and stores balanceOf(PoolManager) of any address that returns 32 bytes (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). After the native payout to the EntryPoint, settle with zero value computes reservesNow - reservesBefore = amount, resets the synced currency and credits that amount under the EntryPoint id (src/PoolManager.sol:356-364). The credit can be minted as a claim (322-329). It can never be paid out, because take would call transfer on the EntryPoint, which reverts, and the transfer check then reverts with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). I looked for a guard that the finding missed and found none that applies: the msg.value check at line 356 only blocks a native settle while an ERC-20 is synced, the int128 cast at line 294 only bounds amount below 2^127, and the delta count check is what forces the caller to pay. I also looked for a way to turn this against other users and found none in core: the recipient of a take is an argument of the caller, the hook split and fee collection never send native value to an address chosen by a third party (src/PoolManager.sol:177-183, 220-226, src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), and the PoolManager balance of ETH ends where it started.
verification.corrections: No change to actor or severity. The actor value unprivileged is right in the sense that no role is needed, and the reader should note that the only party who loses is the account that named the recipient, so this finding gives no path to funds of other users. Three additions. First, the value call succeeds on all seven chains, where the finding reports results for OP Mainnet, Base and Unichain only. Second, take(address(0), L2ToL1MessagePasser, 0) also succeeds, creates no debt because a zero delta is skipped (src/PoolManager.sol:369), and still makes the PoolManager start a zero value withdrawal and raise the message nonce. It carries empty data and the PoolManager address as target, which has no code on Ethereum, so it gives no authority on L1. Third, L1BlockNumber is a proxied predeploy, so the statement that no function pays the ETH out holds for the current implementation, and the chain's proxy admin could change that.

findings.title: A payout sent to an EntryPoint, a precompile address or a protocol custody address is lost to the caller on Arc and Tempo
findings.difference: Arc and Tempo carry addresses that accept a payment from the PoolManager and book it to nobody the caller controls. On Arc the three ERC-4337 EntryPoint contracts accept native USDC with empty calldata and record it as a deposit of the sender. Precompile addresses 0x01 to 0x08 and 0x100, the codeless addresses 0x12 and 0x13 and the system log emitter 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe accept value, and the USDC face accepts a transfer to the Native Coin Authority address and to its own implementation. On Tempo the FeeManager, StablecoinDEX and TIP20ChannelReserve precompile addresses hold TIP-20 balances for their own bookkeeping and accept a plain transfer without crediting an internal account.
findings.mechanism: 1. A caller inside unlock calls take(currency, to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The PoolManager debits the caller's delta by amount and then pays: for address(0) with a value call and empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52), for a token with transfer(to, amount) (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). 2. On Arc, if to is an EntryPoint, the EntryPoint credits a deposit to the PoolManager address. The PoolManager can never call withdrawTo and answers no validation call, so the deposit stays there. If to is 0x01, 0x12, the log emitter or the Native Coin Authority address, the USDC sits at an address without a spending path. 3. On Tempo, if to is 0xfeec..., 0xdec0... or 0x4d5050..., the TIP-20 balance of that precompile address rises by amount and no internal balance of any user is credited. I simulated each of the three with 1 unit of OUSD. I did not find a function that returns such a surplus and did not read the three precompiles in full. 4. In every case the caller still owes amount and must settle it before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 349-364). Pool reserves are whole: amount left and amount came back. 5. A caller who first calls sync(EntryPoint) on Arc, then takes native USDC to the EntryPoint and then calls settle is credited amount under the EntryPoint's address as currency id, because EntryPoint.balanceOf(PoolManager) is the deposit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-360). An eth_call of sync(EntryPoint v0.7) on the deployed PoolManager succeeds. The EntryPoint has no transfer(address,uint256), so that credit can become an ERC-6909 claim and can never be taken.
findings.impact: The amount of each such payout is lost to the party that named the recipient. Other users, pool reserves and claims are not affected. The hazard is real for routers or scripts that let a user name any recipient, and for anyone who accepts ERC-6909 claims under the EntryPoint id.
findings.preconditions: The caller, or a router acting for the caller, must name one of these addresses as recipient. No third party can redirect someone else's payout. On Tempo the native variant does not exist because value transfers fail.
findings.mitigations: Routers and front ends on these two chains can refuse recipients in the precompile ranges, the EntryPoint addresses and the Tempo custody precompiles. Users should not accept ERC-6909 claims whose id is one of these addresses.

findings.title: The USDC implementation address on Arc mirrors the PoolManager's USDC balance, so a third currency id can be credited and never paid out
findings.difference: On Arc the USDC proxy at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 delegates to NativeFiatTokenV2_2 at 0xc6ad664ac6679f4ce74e10e91449c93ec1ae3ca6. The implementation computes balanceOf from the account's native balance divided by 10^12, with no use of its own storage, so a direct call to the implementation returns the same figure as the proxy. Its transfer function calls the Native Coin Authority precompile, which accepts only the proxy address as caller, so a direct transfer on the implementation reverts. An ordinary ERC-20 implementation called directly reports a zero balance.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync(X) accepts any address and stores X.balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). With X set to the implementation address the stored figure is the PoolManager's real USDC balance in 6 decimals, 2,445,327.82 USDC at block 32,584,426. 2. Any USDC that reaches the PoolManager while X is synced, through USDC.transfer on the proxy or through a forced native send, raises X.balanceOf. settle then credits the difference to the caller under currency id X (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). settle with msg.value reverts in that state (src/PoolManager.sol:356). 3. take(X, to, amount) calls transfer on the implementation (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). The precompile rejects the call because its caller is the implementation and the take reverts with ERC20TransferFailed. 4. A positive delta in X can be minted as an ERC-6909 claim, cleared, or used as liquidity in a pool that names X as a currency (src/PoolManager.sol:310-336). None of these turns it back into USDC. 5. The same payment cannot also be credited under 0x3600 or address(0): one sync slot exists, a native credit needs that slot to be zero, and each inflow is counted in one settle. The USDC that was paid in stays in the PoolManager and backs no claim under address(0) or 0x3600.
findings.impact: USDC paid in under the implementation's id is stranded for the payer, and claims or pool positions denominated in that id can never be redeemed. Reserves of address(0) and 0x3600 pools are not reduced. The loss falls on whoever pays into that id or accepts claims in it. A proxy upgrade changes the implementation address and the behaviour of the old one.
findings.preconditions: Someone must sync the implementation address and pay USDC before settling, or accept claims or a pool in that id. An attacker cannot make another user's router sync a different currency than the one it pays.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces on Arc should list address(0) and 0x3600 as the only USDC currency ids and warn on pools or claims whose currency is 0xc6ad664ac6679f4ce74e10e91449c93ec1ae3ca6 or any later implementation address.

findings.title: Source disagrees with two interface comments and two test conditions, and none of the four changes who can move funds
findings.difference: None. These are differences inside the repository, between src and its own comments and tests.
findings.mechanism: First, src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says collectProtocolFees reverts if the contract is unlocked. The code checks only the caller and whether the currency is the synced ERC-20 (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). _isUnlocked is declared at ProtocolFees.sol:60 and implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394 and nothing calls it. The tests agree with the code: they expect ProtocolFeeCurrencySynced in both lock states (test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039). Second, src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 says only initialize and updateDynamicLPFee can be called without unlocking. sync has no onlyWhenUnlocked modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279) and test/Sync.t.sol:36-41 calls it while locked. Third, test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129 expects InvalidFeeForExactOut when amountSpecified >= 0 at a 100 percent fee, while src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-316 reverts only for amountSpecified > 0 and line 320 returns a zero delta for amountSpecified == 0. Fourth, Pool.t.sol:143 treats a zeroForOne price limit below MIN_SQRT_PRICE as out of bounds, while Pool.sol:328 also rejects a limit equal to MIN_SQRT_PRICE. I traced each one for a fund effect. Fee collection inside an unlock changes protocolFeesAccrued and the balance by the same amount and touches no delta. A sync outside an unlock only sets two transient slots that the next sync overwrites. The zero amount swap changes no state. The stricter limit keeps slot0.tick from reaching MIN_TICK - 1.
findings.impact: No loss or freeze found. A reader who trusts the two interface comments gets the wrong picture of when sync and fee collection can run. The fuzz test at Pool.t.sol:129 would fail on an input with amountSpecified equal to zero and a 100 percent fee if the fuzzer produces one.
findings.preconditions: None for the mismatch itself. I could not run forge in this environment, so I do not know whether the current fuzz seed reaches the failing input.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can correct the two comments, decide whether collectProtocolFees should use _isUnlocked or drop it, and align the two test conditions with the source.

These calls show that the deployed contracts accept sync while locked, which is what the code does and what the comment at src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 denies. They do not show what collectProtocolFees does while unlocked, since a read only call cannot open an unlock with the controller as caller. That part rests on the source and the tests. Inside the repository the four mismatches are as the finding states, with the one correction below.
verification.codeCheck: src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says collectProtocolFees reverts if the contract is unlocked. src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52 checks only the caller and the synced ERC-20. _isUnlocked is declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60, implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394 and in two test contracts, and nothing calls it. test/PoolManager.t.sol:1010-1039 attempts collection inside an unlock and expects ProtocolFeeCurrencySynced, so the tests agree with the code. src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 names initialize and updateDynamicLPFee as the only functions callable without unlocking, while sync has no modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279) and test/Sync.t.sol:36-41 calls it directly. test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129 expects InvalidFeeForExactOut for amountSpecified >= 0, while src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-316 reverts only for a positive amount and line 320 returns a zero delta. test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:143 compares with < MIN_SQRT_PRICE and src/libraries/Pool.sol:328 with <=. Collection lowers protocolFeesAccrued and the balance by the same amount (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56), touches no delta and cannot run between sync and settle of the same ERC-20 in either lock state. Fees accrued by a swap that is not yet paid can be collected inside the same unlock, and the unlock reverts as a whole unless the swapper settles (src/PoolManager.sol:112). PoolManager.swap rejects a zero amount (src/PoolManager.sol:193), so Pool.swap sees zero only when a beforeSwap hook delta cancels the amount (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:273-279), and then it changes no state. The stricter price limit stops a swap from ending at MIN_SQRT_PRICE and blocks no withdrawal.

When the limit equals MIN_SQRT_PRICE the test takes neither branch and makes no swap call (test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:135-146), and test/utils/Deployers.sol:43 defines MIN_PRICE_LIMIT as MIN_SQRT_PRICE + 1, which matches the source. The third item is a failing input for the fuzz test whenever the fuzzer picks an LP fee of 1,000,000 together with amountSpecified 0. The setter setIsUnlocked in src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol:27-29 is also unused by any test, which is a further sign that a lock check on fee collection was planned or removed. findings.title: sync runs while the manager is locked and fee collection ignores the lock, and the mainnet fee controller lets anyone trigger collection
findings.difference: On mainnet the protocol fee controller is a V4FeeAdapter contract whose collect and triggerFeeUpdate functions have no access check. Any account can therefore make the PoolManager execute collectProtocolFees and setProtocolFee at a moment it chooses, including inside its own unlock callback. Mainnet also lets several users' operations share one transaction through ERC-4337 bundles and EIP-7702 batches.
findings.mechanism: sync has no onlyWhenUnlocked modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), so anyone can set the synced currency and reserves at any point of a transaction, and the value stays until a settle or another sync in that transaction. collectProtocolFees checks the caller and then reverts only if the currency is an ERC-20 equal to the synced currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). It never calls _isUnlocked, which is declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60 and implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394 with no caller. ASSUMPTIONS.md A12 describes the guard as depending on the unlocked state; the code does not. I walked the fund-moving paths for a gain and found none. Collection of the synced ERC-20 is blocked regardless of lock state, so the balance cannot fall between a sync and its settle through this path. Native settlement uses msg.value and no balance (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354). Collection is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued with checked subtraction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-55) and the adapter fixes the recipient. A sync left behind by an earlier operation in a bundle is overwritten by the next sync and cleared by the next ERC-20 settle (src/PoolManager.sol:361). What remains is that a stale sync makes a later native settle with value revert with NonzeroNativeValue if its caller did not sync first (src/PoolManager.sol:356), and makes collection of that currency revert for the rest of the transaction.
findings.impact: No loss or lasting freeze found. Within one transaction, a party that runs earlier can make a later native settle or a fee collection revert.
findings.preconditions: For the revert cases the two parties must share a transaction, for example an ERC-4337 bundle, and the later party must settle native currency without calling sync first. This is my own reading of the code and has not been checked by a second reviewer.
findings.mitigations: Integrators should call sync immediately before every settle, including native, as the comment at src/PoolManager.sol:348 says. The deployer can decide whether sync should require the unlocked state and whether collectProtocolFees should check it, and can correct the A12 text either way.

The comment at src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says the call reverts if the contract is unlocked. The code and the tests at test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1038 behave otherwise. I traced the fund paths myself. The synced check does not depend on the lock, so collection of a synced ERC-20 always reverts and the balance cannot fall between a sync and its settle through this call. Collection of another currency during an unlock lowers the balance by at most protocolFeesAccrued (checked subtraction at src/ProtocolFees.sol:55) and changes no delta. Fees accrue in _swap before the swapper pays (src/PoolManager.sol:238), and the swapper's negative delta must be cleared before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112) or the whole transaction reverts, collection included. Native settlement credits msg.value only (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354). A collection with the PoolManager as recipient leaves an ERC-20 balance unchanged and reverts for native currency, because src has no receive or fallback function. A sync left by an earlier caller gives a later settler credit only for a real balance increase since that sync, and a native payment then reverts with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356), which test/PoolManager.t.sol:987-988 covers. I found no path that raises a settle credit or pays out more than accrued fees. This agrees with the researcher and answers the researcher's first lead from a second reading.

The repository's own tests expect the present behaviour, so the disagreement is between the code and two texts: the comment at src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 and assumption A12. The synced check as written rejects collection in more situations than a check tied to the lock would, so the difference removes no protection.

findings.title: Operator transaction filtering on Robinhood Chain can fail any exit from the PoolManager, including force-included ones
findings.difference: Ethereum has no party that can make a chosen transaction fail. Robinhood Chain runs the ArbOS 61 compliance filtering feature. Its sequencer drops transactions that involve an address on a restricted list, and an operator account can write any transaction hash into the ArbFilteredTransactionsManager precompile at 0x74. The state transition then skips that transaction, raises the sender's nonce and consumes its gas, even when the transaction was force-included from Ethereum. On chain, filtering has been enabled since 2026-06-24 10:00 UTC and one externally owned account, 0xebdc18a1f5c42fc25552ea233facf4054df224b7 with nonce 6,237, is the registered filterer.
findings.mechanism: Every way to move funds out of the PoolManager is a call made inside unlock: modifyLiquidity with a negative delta, burn of ERC-6909 claims, and take. The contract has no exit that works without a successful child chain transaction. Step 1: the sequencer simulates each transaction and rejects it when it breaks a configured rule. The documented rule types cover a restricted sender or recipient, CALL, CREATE, CREATE2 or SELFDESTRUCT against a restricted address, and token transfers from or to one. Step 2: a user who then sends the transaction through the delayed inbox on Ethereum gets it included after the delay, but the filterer registers its hash first and RevertedTxHook skips the EVM call. The client code checks only whether the hash is in the list, so the list is whatever the filterer writes. Step 3: the user's liquidity and claims stay in the PoolManager with no other route out. The same rules mean that a take to a restricted recipient, or a hook or token that calls a restricted address on every operation, makes the transaction unacceptable to the sequencer. If the PoolManager, the PositionManager, or a widely used token or hook were put on the list, every transaction that calls it would be rejected. I could not confirm which rule set Robinhood has configured or whether any core contract is exempt, because the list is held off chain as salted hashes.
findings.impact: Funds are frozen for the affected sender or contract and cannot be taken by the filterer through this path. At the time of the query the PoolManager on this chain held 21,321 ETH, 16.98M USDG, 1,321 WETH and 3,134 ANT stock tokens. A listing of one LP freezes that LP's positions. A listing of a shared contract freezes every position that depends on it.
findings.preconditions: The filterer account, the compliance list provider or the chain owner must act. No unprivileged party can add a hash or an address. A third party can cause rejection of someone else's transaction only if that transaction already executes code or transfers chosen by the third party, for example a hook that pays out to addresses the third party controls.
findings.mitigations: Nothing in core can restore a forced exit. The deployer can ask the operator for a written commitment that the PoolManager and periphery addresses are never listed and can monitor FilteredTransactionAdded events on 0x74. Pool creators on this chain should avoid hooks that call or pay addresses supplied by third parties. LPs should treat force inclusion as unavailable when sizing positions.

I fetched the Arbitrum compliance filtering page. It describes sequencer simulation against a restricted address list, rule examples for the origin, for CALL, CREATE, CREATE2 and SELFDESTRUCT targets and for token transfers, and a precompile where an authorised account registers the hash of a delayed inbox transaction so that the state transition fails it on inclusion and consumes its gas. I read arbos/tx_processor.go at Nitro v3.11.3. RevertedTxHook reads FilteredTransactions().IsFilteredFree(txHash), raises the sender nonce, sets the remaining gas to zero and returns an error. The caller in core/state_transition.go of the Offchain Labs go-ethereum fork (master branch) skips evm.Call when that error is set. StartTxHook sends a filtered deposit to the filtered funds recipient. I read precompiles/ArbFilteredTransactionsManager.go at v3.11.3. AddFilteredTransaction checks only that the caller is in the filterer set. On chain at Robinhood Chain block 120,625,526 on 2026-11-22: getAllTransactionFilterers() returns one address, 0xebdc18a1f5c42fc25552ea233facf4054df224b7, which has no code and nonce 6,237. getTransactionFilteringFrom() returns 1782295200, which is 2026-06-24 10:00 UTC. getFilteredFundsRecipient() returns 0xbbbd433db8700d8927faaaaf482e007e293ed568. A scan of all logs of address 0x74 from block 0 to the head returns 6,234 FilteredTransactionAdded events, the first on 2026-06-30 and the last on 2026-11-20, and no FilteredTransactionDeleted event. The filter is in regular use. The PoolManager held 21,372 ETH, 16.84M USDG, 1,314 WETH and 3,134 ANT. The ethbeat page says that users can be censored when the operator registers their transaction hash in the precompile, even when the transaction is force-included through the delayed inbox. The only other transfer is collectProtocolFees, which accepts the fee controller alone (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). Liquidity removal and claim burning only create a positive delta for msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184, src/PoolManager.sol:332-336), and unlock reverts unless every delta is cleared (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). Positions are stored under msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161) and a burn of claims needs the holder, an operator or an allowance (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). findings.title: Robinhood Stock Tokens and USDG let the issuer block, pause, burn or upgrade the tokens held by the PoolManager
findings.difference: The assets this chain is built for are issuer-controlled in a more concentrated way than a typical Ethereum token. All Robinhood Stock Tokens are beacon proxies behind one contract, 0xe10b6f6b275de231345c20d14ab812db62151b00, which is both the upgrade beacon and the access registry with isBlocked, blockAccounts, pause and upgradeTo. The shared logic contract has adminBurn(address,uint256) and pause. USDG is an upgradeable Paxos token with isFrozen and decreaseSupplyFromAddress. The PoolManager already holds both.
findings.mechanism: Step 1, block or pause: if the registry blocks the PoolManager address or a token is paused, the token's transfer call fails. Currency.transfer treats a failed call as an error and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed, so every take and every collectProtocolFees in that token reverts. Settling needs a transfer into the PoolManager, which a pause or a block on the recipient would stop as well. One registry entry covers every stock token at once, and A6 applies because one address holds all pools. An LP can still remove liquidity, take the other currency of the pair and call mint to hold the frozen side as an ERC-6909 claim, because mint moves no tokens. The claim cannot be turned into tokens until the block is lifted. Step 2, burn: adminBurn against the PoolManager lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) with no matching delta. Pool reserves, claims and accrued fees then exceed the balance. Takes keep succeeding until the balance runs out, and the last LPs and claim holders bear the shortfall. Step 3, upgrade: upgradeTo on the beacon changes the code of every stock token in one transaction, which removes the A4 expectation that token code is fixed. I read function selectors and view results from chain. I did not read verified source, so the exact transfer check against the registry and the role holders are unconfirmed. Stock token splits and dividends do not create a balance change, because they move uiMultiplier and leave balanceOf fixed.
findings.impact: At the time of the query the PoolManager held 3,134.87 ANT stock tokens and 16,984,261 USDG. A block or pause freezes the stock token side of every pool that uses the affected tokens. A burn creates a loss equal to the burned amount, carried by whoever withdraws last. The other currency in each pair stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The issuer (Robinhood Assets (Jersey) Limited for stock tokens, Paxos for USDG) or a holder of the relevant role must act. isBlocked(PoolManager) and isFrozen(PoolManager) are false today and both tokens are unpaused. No unprivileged party can trigger any of these functions.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can ask both issuers to confirm in writing how the PoolManager address is treated and can monitor the registry and beacon for block, pause and upgrade events. Pool creators and LPs should size stock token and USDG positions with a freeze and a shortfall in mind. A later cycle should read the verified source of the logic and registry contracts.

findings.title: One issuer blocklist entry on the PoolManager address freezes or wipes a stablecoin for every pool
findings.difference: This is a property of assets on mainnet, and mainnet protocol rules are the reference. USDC, USDT and PYUSD each let one issuer role block a single address. USDC blocks transfers from and to a blacklisted address. USDT blocks transfers sent by a blacklisted address and lets the owner call destroyBlackFunds, which sets that address's balance to zero. PYUSD blocks transfers from and to a frozen address and lets the asset protection role call wipeFrozenAddress, which sets the balance to zero.
findings.mechanism: All pools, all ERC-6909 claims and all accrued protocol fees for a currency sit in one token balance at the PoolManager address. take calls currency.transfer and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86), so once the address is blocked nobody can withdraw that token from any pool. collectProtocolFees fails the same way (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). For USDC and PYUSD a transfer into the PoolManager also fails, so settle can no longer be funded in that token (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). For USDT the blocked address can still receive, so users can keep paying USDT in while nothing can leave. If the issuer then zeroes the balance, the pools keep their accounting but the tokens behind it are gone, which is the undercollateralised state described in A2. LPs can still remove liquidity, take the other currency of the pair, and convert the blocked currency's delta into ERC-6909 claims with mint, which does no token transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). The claims stay unredeemable while the block lasts.
findings.impact: At block 26470360 the existing PoolManager holds 79,953,224 USDT, 63,053,277 PYUSD and 30,404,253 USDC. One blocklist transaction per token freezes that token for every LP, every claim holder and the protocol fee balance at once. A wipe by Tether or Paxos turns the freeze into a loss of the full balance. The other currency of each affected pool stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The issuer role must act: the USDC blacklister (0x0a06be16275b95a7d2567fbdae118b36c7da78f9), the USDT owner (0xc6cde7c39eb2f0f0095f41570af89efc2c1ea828) or a PYUSD ASSET_PROTECTION_ROLE holder. The PoolManager is not blocked on any of the three today. I found no way for an unprivileged party to cause the block directly. I did not research what legal or policy triggers each issuer applies to contract addresses.
findings.mitigations: The deployer cannot remove this from a singleton. Interfaces and LPs can treat issuer-controlled tokens as carrying whole-protocol exposure instead of per-pool exposure. Monitoring isBlacklisted, isBlackListed and isFrozen for the PoolManager address gives early warning. Routers can fall back to ERC-6909 claims for settlement when token transfers to the PoolManager fail.

findings.title: Role holders on GHO, syrupUSDC, apxUSD, shMON and mUSD can pause, burn, move or replace balances that the Monad PoolManager holds
findings.difference: Five further tokens with issuer controls sit at the single PoolManager address on Monad, next to the dollar tokens that F-015 already lists. The PoolManager holds 2,729,903 GHO, 1,645,837 mUSD, 1,561,546 syrupUSDC, 299,944 apxUSD and 269,214 shMON.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager records what each pool is owed and trusts balanceOf to stay equal to the sum. GHO, apxUSD, shMON and mUSD are proxies, so the party that controls the proxy can replace the token logic. The apxUSD and mUSD implementations contain pause, and a paused token makes every take of that currency revert at src/types/Currency.sol:73-86, which stops removals and swaps in every pool that uses it. The syrupUSDC and apxUSD code contains burn(address,uint256), and the mUSD implementation contains forceTransfer(address,address,uint256) and freeze. If the role holder applies one of them to the PoolManager address, the balance falls while the pool accounting stays unchanged, and the last liquidity providers to withdraw cannot be paid. This reading rests on the selectors found in the deployed bytecode. Which accounts hold the roles, and whether burn(address,uint256) needs an allowance, was not confirmed.
findings.impact: All pools on Monad that use the affected token. The amounts at the time of the query are listed above: about 6.2 million units of dollar tokens and 269,214 shMON.
findings.preconditions: The issuer or the holder of the relevant role acts against the PoolManager address or pauses or upgrades the token. An ordinary account cannot trigger it.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers can weigh the issuer controls of each token before they supply it. The deployer cannot remove the dependency, because one address holds the balances of every pool.

Its implementation holds the selectors of pause(), unpause(), freeze(address), forceTransfer(address,address,uint256) and the batch form of forceTransfer. paused() and isFrozen(PoolManager) both return false. syrupUSDC at 0xab6e5a0c3799d020c790d34f7b2c02639e238af7 has no proxy slot and holds the selectors of mint(address,uint256), burn(address,uint256), burnFrom(address,uint256) and BURNER_ROLE(). apxUSD at 0x3d78455e22d5dd49709ec135a59cb1c5a87ac3c6 is a 163 byte proxy with implementation 0x6b3788fd6604bbf03c5378d24e57bb334baad4af, which holds pause(), unpause(), burn(address,uint256), burnFrom(address,uint256) and upgradeToAndCall(address,bytes). paused() returns false. shMON at 0x1b68626dca36c7fe922fd2d55e4f631d962de19c is a proxy with a 120,874 byte implementation that holds upgradeTo(address), and owner() returns 0x48a3267bcc4cf230e9bc4cae0c11eebdb9a6a687. Its EIP-1967 admin slot holds 0x00b16590295092f12f4cec655296b6129c49489c, which the finding does not mention. I computed each selector with keccak256 and searched the deployed bytecode for it. As in the finding, the holders of the roles were not read, and I did not establish whether burn(address,uint256) needs an allowance or whether forceTransfer on mUSD applies only to frozen accounts. Those points decide between a pause and a loss. They do not change the actor or the fact that the controls exist.
verification.codeCheck: A token payout is one call to transfer, and take reverts when that call reverts or returns anything other than nothing or a 32 byte true (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86, src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). A token payment is measured as balanceOf(PoolManager) minus the synced value (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364), so a token that blocks transfers to the PoolManager also blocks payments. The PoolManager stores no reserve per currency. Pool state is liquidity, price and fee growth (src/libraries/Pool.sol:83-91), and claims are ERC-6909 balances (src/ERC6909.sol:15-19). A burn or forced transfer of the PoolManager balance therefore changes no accounting, and the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws last, because their take reverts in the token for lack of balance. One guard reduces the pause case. modifyLiquidity and swap only write deltas (src/PoolManager.sol:145-227), and mint and burn close deltas through ERC-6909 claims without any call to the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). During a pause or a freeze of the PoolManager address a provider can still remove liquidity into claims and a swapper can still trade from and into claims. The token itself cannot enter or leave the PoolManager until the issuer lifts the measure.
verification.corrections: The mechanism says a paused token stops removals and swaps in every pool that uses it. The code stops take and settle for that currency. Removals and swaps that are closed with mint and burn of ERC-6909 claims continue (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336), so the effect of a pause is that the token cannot be paid out or paid in. The balances at block 124498672 are 2,640,693 GHO, 1,650,963 mUSD, 1,561,546 syrupUSDC, 299,944 apxUSD and 268,856 shMON. shMON has a proxy admin at 0x00b16590295092f12f4cec655296b6129c49489c in addition to the owner named in the finding. The actor value issuer is correct. No step is open to an ordinary account.

findings.title: USDC and USDT0 issuers can block the PoolManager address, which stops every pool in that currency, and USDT0's owner can burn the blocked balance
findings.difference: Ethereum has the same class of issuer control for USDC, so this is a property of the assets pools hold on HyperEVM and is listed for completeness of the per network picture. On HyperEVM the two main stablecoins are native Circle USDC at 0xb88339CB7199b77E23DB6E890353E22632Ba630f and USDT0 at 0xB8CE59FC3717ada4C02eaDF9682A9e934F625ebb. USDC has a blacklister role (0x33aa4e959132e49552cb754fb6585bdcdf874beb) and a pauser, and a blacklisted address can neither send nor receive. USDT0 has an owner (0xb64a89ad247a2d691a728bb6822a85eedd7fc541) that maintains a blocklist and can call destroyBlockedFunds on a blocked address. Both tokens sit behind upgradeable proxies. USDC is also the asset HyperCore treats specially under AQAv2, which raises the share of pool liquidity likely to sit in it.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, all ERC-6909 claims and all protocol fees in one currency share one token balance at the PoolManager address. 2. Every payout runs take, which calls transfer on the token with the PoolManager as sender and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 3. If the USDC blacklister lists the PoolManager, or the USDC pauser pauses the token, every USDC transfer from or to the PoolManager reverts. take of USDC fails for all pools and inbound payment fails too, so the balance check in settle never sees new funds (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365). 4. If the USDT0 owner blocks the PoolManager, transfers out revert while transfers in still succeed, so users can pay in and nobody can take out. The owner can then call destroyBlockedFunds and burn the whole PoolManager balance. Pool state still says the tokens are owed, and every later take of USDT0 fails for lack of balance. 5. modifyLiquidity and swap only move deltas (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184 and 187-227). An LP can still remove liquidity, take the other currency and call mint to hold the blocked currency as an ERC-6909 claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). The claim is redeemable only if the block is lifted.
findings.impact: All USDC or all USDT0 held by the PoolManager across every pool, plus claims and protocol fees in that currency. A block freezes them. destroyBlockedFunds on USDT0 removes them for good. The other currency of each affected pool stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The token issuer acts against the PoolManager address: Circle's blacklister or pauser for USDC, the USDT0 owner for USDT0, or the proxy admin of either token through an upgrade. No unprivileged party can trigger this. On-chain reads at block 51,941,800 show isBlacklisted(PoolManager) false, paused() false and isBlocked(PoolManager) false.
findings.mitigations: The deployer cannot remove the control. LPs can limit exposure by choosing pool pairs with that risk in mind. Front ends can watch for Blacklisted and BlockPlaced events that name the PoolManager and tell LPs to exit the other side of each pool with take and to hold the blocked side with mint. Integrators should not treat ERC-6909 claims in these currencies as equal to the token while a block is in force.

sources.supports: A blacklisted address cannot call transfer or transferFrom and cannot receive tokens. The blacklister role controls the list and the pauser can stop all transfers.
The USDT0 contract owner maintains an on-chain isBlocked list, blocked addresses cannot send tokens, and the tokens sit behind upgradeable proxies.
The USDT0 owner can block accounts and burn tokens from blocked accounts. Blocked accounts can still receive transfers.

Nothing in src/ offers a second way to move a token out, so a block on the PoolManager address stops take for every pool in that currency. _settle credits only the balance increase since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), so a token that rejects inbound transfers cannot be paid in. The partial exit holds: modifyLiquidity and swap only write deltas (src/PoolManager.sol:181-183 and 224-226), and mint debits the delta and writes an ERC-6909 balance without calling the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329, src/ERC6909.sol:79-83). No guard was missed. No test models a blocking token. test_take_failsWithInvalidTokensThatDoNotReturnTrueOnTransfer (test/PoolManager.t.sol:924) covers the revert when the token call does not return true.

The hazard exists in the same form on Ethereum, as the finding says, so it is a property of the pooled assets and not of the HyperEVM execution layer. findings.title: Celo governance can move native CELO out of the PoolManager through the CELO token proxy and the transfer precompile
findings.difference: On Ethereum no contract can debit ETH from another account. On Celo a precompile at 0xfd transfers native CELO from any address named in its input to any other address. The precompile accepts calls only from the CELO token address 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438. That address is an upgradeable proxy owned by the Celo Governance contract.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager keeps native CELO as its own account balance. Pools that use currency address(0) and pools that use the CELO token address both draw on that balance (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96, and the on-chain balances are equal). The precompile reads the debited account from its first argument and checks only the caller. The current token implementation passes msg.sender or an allowance checked from address. A new implementation installed through _setImplementation could pass the PoolManager address as from and any recipient as to. The PoolManager has no code that runs on such a debit and no way to veto it. After the debit, take for either CELO currency pays out until the balance is exhausted (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), so the last LPs to withdraw bear the loss. A new implementation that makes transfer revert would freeze every pool that uses the CELO token address, because take calls transfer on it (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). Pools that use address(0) would still pay out by value transfer in that case. Governance returns stage durations of 1 day, 7 days and 3 days, which this review reads as approval, referendum and execution, so a standard proposal is public for days before it can execute. The hotfix path needs the approver multisig and the Security Council and has a 1 day execution window with no referendum.
findings.impact: All native CELO in the PoolManager, 6,167.7 CELO at the time of the query, across both currency faces. Every CELO holder on the chain carries the same exposure. Other tokens in the PoolManager are not reachable by this path.
findings.preconditions: A Celo governance proposal or a hotfix approved by the approver multisig and the Security Council must replace the CELO token implementation. No unprivileged path was found: an eth_call to the precompile from an address other than the token fails, and _setImplementation reverts for a sender other than Governance.
findings.mitigations: Watch the value of _getImplementation() on the CELO token proxy and the Governance contract for queued proposals and hotfixes that target 0x471E...a438. The referendum stage gives LPs days to withdraw before a standard proposal executes. A hotfix gives no such window. LPs who want protection from a token contract that reverts can use pools with currency address(0), which pay out without calling the token.

The precompile manipulates balances in the state database directly and can only be called by the CELO token.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the celo-kona precompile source. The transfer precompile sits at 0xff minus 2, which is 0xfd. It halts unless the caller equals the chain's CELO token address, then reads from, to and value from a 96 byte input and calls the internal transfer between those two accounts. Nothing ties from to the account that called the token. The former op-geth client does the same in celo_contracts.go: IsCallerCeloToken, then a transfer between the decoded from and to. The Celo token duality page says the precompile changes balances in the state database and can only be called by the CELO token. On chain at Celo block 83,451,124: _getOwner() on 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 returns 0xD533Ca259b330c7A88f74E000a3FaEa2d63B7972, and the registry at 0x000000000000000000000000000000000000ce10 returns that address for Governance and the token address for GoldToken and CeloToken. _getImplementation() returns 0xFeA1B35f1D5f2A58532a70e7A32e6F2D3Bc4F7B1 and getVersionNumber() returns 1, 2, 0, 0. eth_getBalance of the PoolManager and CELO.balanceOf(PoolManager) both return 6166941836241617055206 wei. An eth_call of _setImplementation from Governance returns and the same call from 0xA1 reverts with 'sender was not owner'. An eth_call to 0xfd with input (PoolManager, 0xA1, 1) succeeds when the caller is the token address and fails with a precompile error when the caller is 0x01. The GoldToken source on the monorepo master branch passes msg.sender in transfer and an allowance checked from in transferFrom. That source reports version 1.3.0.0 and the deployed implementation reports 1.2.0.0, so I could not match the deployed code line by line. Governance.stageDurations() returns 86,400, 604,800 and 259,200 seconds. Proposals.sol on master declares the struct fields in the order approval, referendum, execution, which settles the reading the researcher left open. hotfixExecutionTimeWindow() returns 86,400. In Governance.sol approveHotfix accepts the approver or the Security Council, prepareHotfix requires both approvals, and executeHotfix requires both and an unexpired time limit. No referendum is involved. approver() is a contract whose required() returns 3 and whose getOwners() returns 14 addresses. securityCouncil() is 0x51a3a77bAF58FEf0309452ceacB09221E556F223, which has no code on Celo and equals the Ethereum Safe 0x4092A77bAF58fef0309452cEaCb09221e556E112 plus the alias offset. That Safe has threshold 2 and two owners, each a Safe with threshold 6 and 8 owners.
verification.codeCheck: balanceOfSelf returns address(this).balance for address(0) and token.balanceOf(address(this)) for any other currency (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). On Celo both expressions read the same number, so pools on address(0) and pools on the CELO token share one balance. take debits the caller's delta and then calls transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The native branch is a call with value that reverts with NativeTransferFailed when it fails (src/types/Currency.sol:45-53), so after an outside debit takes succeed until the balance runs out and later ones revert. The token branch calls transfer(address,uint256) on the currency and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed on failure (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86), so an implementation whose transfer reverts blocks every take of the token currency. sync on the token calls balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). I looked for a guard and found none. The contract has no receive or fallback function and the only payable functions are settle and settleFor (src/PoolManager.sol:300 and 305). Nothing in src/ compares the balance with pool accounting outside the sync and settle pair. The delta count check at the end of unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:112) covers one transaction and cannot see a debit made by another contract. I also looked for an unprivileged route to the same debit. The PoolManager calls only transfer and balanceOf on a currency, so it never grants a token allowance and transferFrom cannot debit it. The token address cannot be used as a hook: its low 14 bits are 0x2438, which sets the before swap returns delta flag without the before swap flag, and isValidHookAddress rejects that (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:111). test/Sync.t.sol:255-276 covers a settle with value while a NativeERC20 is synced. No test models a third party debit of the manager's native balance or a change of token implementation.
verification.corrections: 1. The impact is wider than stated for pools that list the CELO token as a currency. A replaced implementation could report a larger balanceOf between sync and settle. _settle credits the difference to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364), and the caller can swap that credit for the paired currency in every pool that lists the CELO token and take it out. The statement that other tokens are not reachable holds for the precompile debit alone. Pools on address(0) are exposed to the precompile debit alone. 2. The hotfix path needs 3 of 14 approver signers and the Security Council. The Security Council address is the alias of the Ethereum Safe that also owns Celo's ProxyAdmin on both layers, so one signer set sits in the predeploy upgrade path and in the CELO token hotfix path. 3. If transfer reverts, an LP in a CELO token pool can still turn a positive delta into ERC-6909 claims with mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), which makes no token call. The claim stays inside the PoolManager, so this is bookkeeping and gives no exit. 4. The balance was 6,166.94 CELO at my read against 6,167.7 in the finding. 5. Severity stays high because the actor is chain governance. The exposure today is small and is shared by every CELO holder.

findings.title: B20 precompile tokens on Base give the issuer seize, pause and policy control over the PoolManager balance, and their rules change at hard forks
findings.difference: Since the Beryl upgrade on 25 June 2026, Base has a native token standard called B20. Anyone can create a token through a factory precompile at 0xB20f000000000000000000000000000000000000, and all B20 tokens share logic that runs natively in the node. Each token has role gated mint, burn and seizeWithMemo, a pause switch per feature, and policy slots that are checked on every transfer against the sender, the receiver and msg.sender. The policies are allowlists or blocklists stored in a shared Policy Registry precompile, and one policy can back many tokens and be administered by a third party. Base changes the shared logic at hard forks: Cobalt added seize, and Denim on 5 November 2026 started to enforce the executor policy on plain transfer calls. Ethereum has no enshrined token logic of this kind.
findings.mechanism: 1. A pool is created with a B20 token as one currency. Users pay in with sync, a token transfer and settle, which credits balanceOf(PoolManager) minus the synced reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364). 2. Every payout calls transfer on the token with the PoolManager as msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). For a B20 token that call passes through the TRANSFER pause check, then TRANSFER_EXECUTOR_POLICY on msg.sender, TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY on from, and TRANSFER_RECEIVER_POLICY on to. msg.sender and from are both the PoolManager. 3. If the token admin pauses TRANSFER, binds a policy that does not authorise the PoolManager, or the admin of a referenced policy removes the PoolManager from an allowlist or adds it to a blocklist, the transfer reverts and take reverts with ERC20TransferFailed. Every pool, every ERC-6909 claim and the protocol fee balance in that currency are stuck together because they share one holder address. collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer path (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 4. If the issuer has configured SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY so that the PoolManager is not exempt, an account with SEIZE_ROLE can call seizeWithMemo(PoolManager, to, amount, memo). The seize skips allowances and the three transfer policies. The PoolManager balance falls without any delta being recorded, so the pools hold less than their accounting says, and the last LPs and claim holders to withdraw cannot be paid. 5. A hard fork can produce the freeze in step 3 with no action by the issuer after pool creation. Before Denim a token with a restrictive executor allowlist still allowed holder initiated transfer, so the PoolManager could pay out. Since Denim the same token rejects transfer from any msg.sender that is not on the executor allowlist. 6. A seize or pause in the middle of a settlement cannot be turned into credit: a lower balance makes reservesNow minus reservesBefore underflow and revert (src/PoolManager.sol:360).
findings.impact: All liquidity, ERC-6909 claims and accrued protocol fees held in the affected B20 token on Base. A seize is a direct loss for LPs of that token. A pause or policy change freezes the token side of every pool that uses it. The other currency of each pool is not affected. Which B20 tokens the Base PoolManager holds today, and in what amounts, could not be listed in this cycle because the public RPC rate limited log queries and the Base explorer blocked the request. The PoolManager's ETH, WETH and USDC on Base are not B20 tokens: the factory returns false for isB20(USDC).
findings.preconditions: A B20 token with market value is used in v4 pools on Base. For a freeze, the token admin, the pauser, or the admin of a policy the token references must act, or a Base hard fork must tighten enforcement for a configuration the token already has. For a seize, the issuer must hold SEIZE_ROLE and must have set SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY to a policy that does not authorise the PoolManager. With the slot unset no account is seizable. An unprivileged attacker cannot do any of this to a token issued by someone else. An attacker who issues their own B20 token gets no more than a hostile ERC-20 already gives on any chain.
findings.mitigations: Pool creators and LPs should read, for every B20 currency, the three transfer policy slots, the seize policy slots, the holders of DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, SEIZE_ROLE and PAUSE_ROLE, and the admin of each referenced policy, and should treat a non renounced admin as able to freeze or seize. Front ends and routers on Base can call isAuthorized on the Policy Registry for the PoolManager under each bound policy and warn when it is false or when the policy admin is live. LPs caught by a freeze can still remove liquidity and keep the frozen side as ERC-6909 claims through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), which does not call the token, and take the other currency. The deployer should track each Base upgrade changelog for B20 changes before activation.

sources.supports: B20 runs as precompiles in the Base node, is upgraded through hard forks, is created by anyone through the factory, and has roles, pause vectors and policies.

verification.factCheck: All six Base docs pages were fetched and say what the finding reports. The upgrades page lists Beryl on 25 June 2026, Cobalt on 30 September 2026 and Denim on 5 November 2026 for Base Mainnet. The introduction states that B20 runs as precompiles in the node, that Base upgrades the logic through hard forks, that every token is created through the factory, and that TRANSFER, MINT, BURN and SEIZE can be paused separately. The policies page gives the scope table: sender policy on from, receiver policy on to, executor policy on msg.sender, and a policy admin who can change membership for every token that references the policy. The Cobalt note confirms that seizeWithMemo skips allowances and the three transfer policies and that an unset SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY makes no account seizable. The Denim note confirms that the executor policy now runs on transfer and calls the change breaking for tokens with a restrictive executor policy. On chain at Base block 60,794,561 on 22 November 2026: eth_getCode at the factory is empty, isB20(PoolManager) and isB20(USDC) return false, policyExists(2) returns true, and balanceOf and transfer on the uninitialised address 0xb200000000000000000001000000000000000001 revert. I also closed the gap the finding left open about exposure. The explorer lists recent transfers between the PoolManager and two B20 tokens. OUSD (name OpenUSD, 0xB2000000000000000000002fEb517dFeC7415344, isB20 true, code 0xef, 6 decimals): balanceOf(PoolManager) is 5,341,029 of a total supply of 93,186,135. Its TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY is policy 122, whose admin 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246 has no code. The other five scopes are unset, pausedFeatures is empty, and the PoolManager is authorised under policy 122 today. AMDC (name Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 0xB2000000000000000000000d8Ce462E99ee7A47B, 8 decimals): balanceOf(PoolManager) is 34.38. Policy 5 (admin 0xec0f05c174e54fbf0fe16ad930a8afebce612812) is bound to the sender, receiver, executor and mint receiver scopes, and SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY is policy 129 (admin 0x38467be00970af18076fd08f6b4cf38ba91572b1). The PoolManager is authorised under both today, so it can transfer and is seize exempt. Not confirmed: who holds DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, PAUSE_ROLE, SEIZE_ROLE and BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE on either token, because the public endpoints refused archive log queries. The list of B20 tokens at the PoolManager is a sample of the 50 latest transfers and is incomplete.
verification.codeCheck: sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) for the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). _settle credits balanceOf minus the stored reserves with checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), so a balance that fell between sync and settle reverts and gives no credit. take records the negative delta and then calls transfer with the PoolManager as msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). A reverting token call ends in a revert that wraps ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). No storage in src/ tracks reserves per currency: every payout depends on the live token balance, so a seize or burn of the PoolManager balance is not detected and the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws last. mint and burn of ERC-6909 claims do not call the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336), and modifyLiquidity does not call it either (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184), so the claim based exit in the mitigations works at the core level. The balanceOf call decodes return data, and the transfer call is a raw call with no code size check, so a token whose code is the single byte 0xef works with this code. The live OUSD balance supports that. Tests cover a transfer that fails (test/PoolManager.t.sol:924-957) and a balance that only grows between sync and settle (test/Sync.t.sol:82-253). No test in test/ models a token that pauses, blocks the PoolManager, or lowers its balance from outside.
verification.corrections: 1. The finding misses a second loss path. burnBlocked(from, amount) has existed since Beryl and is still callable. It destroys the balance of a holder that is not authorised under TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY, and it needs BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE and an unpaused BURN feature. It does not read SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY. The statement that no balance can be removed while the seize slot is unset is therefore too strong: an issuer who blocks the PoolManager under the sender policy and holds BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE can burn its balance. OUSD has a sender policy bound, so this path applies to it if that role is granted. 2. The exposure is no longer hypothetical. The PoolManager holds about 5.34 million OUSD, and one account without code administers the policy that decides whether the PoolManager may send it. 3. take reverts with WrappedError that carries ERC20TransferFailed as context. 4. The claim based exit needs a caller whose unlock callback can call mint. Whether the deployed position manager offers that is outside this repository and was not checked. 5. The fork driven freeze in step 5 is a documented behaviour change. Neither of the two tokens found at the PoolManager has an executor allowlist that excludes it, so no instance of that freeze was observed. 6. PAUSE_ROLE, not the admin role, is what pauses TRANSFER. The admin can grant it.

findings.title: Blacklist and freeze roles on the pooled stablecoins can stop every pool that holds them, because one address holds all balances
findings.difference: The issuer model matches USDC on Ethereum, but the role holders are set per chain and several of the largest PoolManager balances in this unit are tokens that Ethereum pools do not hold in this form. On Soneium the bridged USDC.e returns one address, 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59, for owner, pauser and blacklister. On Ink and Unichain USD₮0 exposes isBlocked. On Ink USDG and on Soneium USDSC expose isFrozen. Circle USDC on OP Mainnet, Base, Unichain, World Chain and Ink each has its own blacklister and pauser address.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees for a currency sit in one token balance at the PoolManager address. 2. FiatToken transfer carries the modifiers whenNotPaused, notBlacklisted(msg.sender) and notBlacklisted(to). When the PoolManager pays out, it is msg.sender (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86, called from src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 and src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 3. If the blacklister lists the PoolManager address, or the pauser pauses the token, every take of that currency reverts with ERC20TransferFailed. sync still works because balanceOf is a view call. 4. The freeze covers every pool on the chain that uses the token, regardless of which pool or user caused the listing. 5. The freeze functions on USD₮0, USDG and USDSC were confirmed to exist by eth_call. Their effect on transfers and any balance destroying function were not read from source in this cycle.
findings.impact: At read time the PoolManager held about 12.25 million USDC on Base, 978,360 USDC and 180,746 USD₮0 on Unichain, 1.52 million USD₮0, 767,333 USDG and 676,274 USDC on Ink, 1.90 million USDSC and 517,001 USDC.e on Soneium, 323,556 USDC on OP Mainnet and 66,644 USDC on World Chain. A listing of the PoolManager freezes the whole balance of that token for all LPs, claim holders and the protocol. isBlacklisted, isBlocked or isFrozen returned false for the PoolManager on every token checked.
findings.preconditions: The token's blacklister, freezer or pauser acts against the PoolManager address or pauses the token. This is a privileged issuer action. An unprivileged attacker cannot trigger it directly. A realistic trigger is a compliance response to tainted funds that were routed through a pool.
findings.mitigations: LPs can exit the non frozen currency normally and hold the frozen currency as ERC-6909 claims through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329) until the listing is lifted. Integrators should monitor the blacklist and pause state of each large pooled token for the PoolManager address on each chain. For Soneium USDC.e, the deployer should identify who controls 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59 before treating it like Circle issued USDC.

verification.factCheck: The Circle source was fetched: FiatTokenV1.transfer carries whenNotPaused, notBlacklisted(msg.sender) and notBlacklisted(to) (lines 287-293), and transferFrom also checks from. I repeated the on-chain reads on 22 November 2026. Soneium USDC.e returns 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59 for owner, pauser and blacklister. Blacklister addresses on OP Mainnet, Base, Unichain, World Chain and Ink match the finding. isBlacklisted, isBlocked and isFrozen return false for the PoolManager on every token, and paused is false where the call exists. Balances at the PoolManager: 12.57 million USDC on Base, 980,196 USDC and 180,760 USD₮0 on Unichain, 1.53 million USD₮0, 779,410 USDG and 767,378 USDC on Ink, 1.90 million USDSC and 516,436 USDC.e on Soneium, 335,159 USDC on OP Mainnet and 66,519 USDC on World Chain. These are within normal drift of the figures in the finding. One link is weaker than stated: the Base USDC and Soneium USDC.e proxies report version 2 and point to a 23,464 byte implementation, and I read only the V1 source. The implementation bytecode contains the blacklist(address) selector, so the list exists there. I did not read that the later version keeps the same three modifiers on transfer. For USDG the isFrozen call answers, but I did not find the freeze selectors in the implementation behind the EIP-1967 slot, so where that logic lives was not established.
verification.codeCheck: Every payout of an ERC-20 currency is a transfer call made by the PoolManager (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86), reached from take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). There is one holder address for all pools, claims and fees, so a listing of that address or a token pause makes each of these calls revert. sync only reads balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:285), which the Circle source does not gate. A listed PoolManager also cannot receive, because transfer checks the recipient, so a settle that follows a token transfer fails as well. mint and burn of ERC-6909 claims do not touch the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336), so positions can still be closed into claims and swaps can still be settled in claims. No guard in src/ was missed. test/ has no case for a paused or blacklisting token.
verification.corrections: 1. The effect is understated for USD₮0. The USD₮0 implementations on Unichain (0xaf37e8b6c9ed7f6318979f56fc287d76c30847ff) and Ink (0x06d886ff518b5e642e7e6aad3ce797b7dabd8e9a) contain the selectors of addToBlockedList(address) and destroyBlockedFunds(address). A blocked PoolManager could therefore lose its whole USD₮0 balance, about 1.53 million on Ink and 180,760 on Unichain, which is a loss for LPs and claim holders. I matched selectors in bytecode and did not read the source or the access control. USDSC on Soneium has freeze and unfreeze and none of the wipe selectors I tried. 2. The difference from Ethereum is thin. The Ethereum PoolManager is exposed to the same issuer roles. What is specific to this unit is the set of role holders and balances, and the single account behind all three roles of Soneium USDC.e. 3. The claim based exit depends on the contract that owns the position being able to call mint in its unlock callback. That was not checked. 4. Severity stays high: the actor is a token issuer and the frozen amount is the full balance of the token across all pools.

findings.title: TIP-20 issuer roles can burn, freeze or pause the PoolManager balance of a Tempo stablecoin
findings.difference: On Tempo every stablecoin is a TIP-20 precompile with issuer roles built into the protocol. burnAt(from, amount), live on mainnet since T12 on 13 October 2026, lets a BURN_AT_ROLE holder burn any balance with no transfer policy check, unless the holder is on a protected list. burnBlocked lets a BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE holder burn the balance of an address that fails the sender policy. The protected list is FeeManager, StablecoinDEX, TIP20ChannelReserve, ReceivePolicyGuard, the token's own address and Zone Portal addresses. The PoolManager is not on it. pause stops every transfer of the token. The admin of a TIP-403 policy can block an address for every token bound to that policy, and pathUSD and OUSD are both bound to policy 2, a blacklist administered by 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246. Ethereum has no protocol-level burn of another account's ERC-20 balance. Each token there has whatever controls its own contract code contains.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees for a token sit in one TIP-20 balance at the PoolManager address. 2. A BURN_AT_ROLE holder calls burnAt(PoolManager, x). The TIP-20 precompile debits the PoolManager and reduces total supply. No PoolManager function runs. 3. The PoolManager tracks no per-currency reserve in storage. sync reads balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) and take pays out with transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75), so the claims recorded in pool state and ERC-6909 balances now exceed the tokens held. Withdrawals succeed until the balance runs out, then transfer reverts with InsufficientBalance and the remaining LPs and claim holders cannot exit. 4. The freeze variant: the policy admin adds the PoolManager to blacklist policy 2, or a PAUSE_ROLE holder pauses the token. Every take and every inbound payment for that token then reverts with PolicyForbids or ContractPaused, and settle cannot complete because the payment transfer fails. Once the PoolManager fails the sender policy, a BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE holder can also burn its balance. 5. If a burn lands between sync and settle inside one transaction, the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 reverts that transaction and nothing else changes.
findings.impact: At block 50,261,382 the PoolManager held about 406,197 OUSD and 19,727 pathUSD. A burn destroys part of the shared balance and the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws last, across every pool that uses the token. A blacklist entry or a pause freezes the full balance of that token, and policy 2 covers pathUSD and OUSD at once.
findings.preconditions: A holder of BURN_AT_ROLE, BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE or PAUSE_ROLE on the token, the token admin, or the admin of the TIP-403 policy must act. An unprivileged attacker has these roles only on tokens they created through the TIP-20 factory, which harms only pools that chose to hold that token. I could not list the current holders of BURN_AT_ROLE and BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE on OUSD and pathUSD, because the public RPC limits log queries to 100,000 blocks. I confirmed that both role constants exist on both tokens, that both tokens use policy 2, and that the PoolManager is authorized under policy 2 today.
findings.mitigations: LPs should treat every TIP-20 as an asset its issuer can burn or freeze at the PoolManager address, and check role holders and the policy admin before providing liquidity. The deployer can ask Tempo to add the PoolManager to the protected address list for burnAt and burnBlocked, and can ask issuers to confirm in writing that the PoolManager will not be blacklisted. Interfaces can warn when a pool token has a BURN_AT_ROLE holder.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the TIP-20 specification, the T12 upgrade page, the TIP-403 specification and the upgrade schedule. They say what the finding says. burnAt(from, amount) requires BURN_AT_ROLE and an unpaused token, ignores transfer policy authorization, debits from and reduces total supply. burnBlocked requires the source to fail the sender policy. Both reject FeeManager, StablecoinDEX, TIP20ChannelReserve, ReceivePolicyGuard, the token's own address and Zone Portal addresses with ProtectedAddress. T12 went live on mainnet on 13 October 2026. I read the client source on the main branch. burn_at calls check_not_paused, check_role, check_burn_address and then moves the balance to the zero address. The PROTECTED list holds only the four system addresses, and check_burn_address adds the token itself and the Zone Portal prefix. The PoolManager address matches none of them. On chain between blocks 50,274,136 and 50,275,429: pathUSD (0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000000000) and OUSD (0x20c0000000000000000000006a37da5c996874be) both return transferPolicyId 2. policyData(2) returns type 1 and admin 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246. isAuthorized(2, PoolManager) returns true. balanceOf(PoolManager) was 403,954.29 OUSD and 19,644.52 pathUSD. I then ran three read-only simulations with eth_simulateV1 against live state. In the first, 0x79c6631fa15cda38777fb9dd7a6348baee794a4e grants itself BURN_AT_ROLE and calls burnAt(PoolManager, 1). Both calls succeed on OUSD and on pathUSD, and balanceOf(PoolManager) falls by one unit. In the second, the same account grants itself PAUSE_ROLE and calls pause, after which transfer from the PoolManager reverts with ContractPaused on both tokens. In the third, 0x251d2711...5246 calls modifyPolicyBlacklist(2, PoolManager, true), after which isAuthorized(2, PoolManager) returns false, transfers from the PoolManager revert with PolicyForbids on both tokens, and a transfer to the PoolManager reverts with PolicyForbids. No transaction was sent.
verification.codeCheck: sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) in transient storage and nothing in persistent storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). take debits the caller's delta and calls transfer with no comparison against any recorded reserve (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). A failed token call reverts the take with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). No function in src/ observes a balance that fell outside take or collectProtocolFees, so a burn leaves pool state and ERC-6909 balances above the tokens held and the last withdrawers meet InsufficientBalance. After a blacklist entry or a pause, take reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, a payer cannot move tokens to the PoolManager so _settle credits zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364), and collectProtocolFees reverts at src/ProtocolFees.sol:56. A burn between sync and settle in one transaction makes the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 revert. I found no guard the finding missed. The tests do not cover this case. A search of test/ and src/test/ finds no token mock with an issuer burn, a blacklist or a pause.
verification.corrections: The finding could not list role holders. I read every RoleMembershipUpdated log on both tokens from block 0 to block 50,274,300 in 100,000 block windows. There are 16 events, and none grants BURN_AT_ROLE, BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE, PAUSE_ROLE or UNPAUSE_ROLE. hasRole returns false for those roles on every account that appears in the logs. So nobody holds a burn or pause role on OUSD today. pathUSD had one admin set at genesis without an event, so I cannot exclude a genesis holder there. The roles are one transaction away. 0x79c6631f...4a4e holds DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on both tokens, getRoleAdmin returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE for all of them, and the simulation shows it can grant itself a role and use it. That account and the policy 2 admin both carry 23 bytes of code, the EIP-7702 designator 0xef0100 followed by 0x000000fb7702036ff9f76044a501ac1aa74cbab16b. They are signer-controlled accounts and I did not find out how many signers control them. Step 4 says every pool operation stops. The transfers stop. Swaps and liquidity changes that settle with ERC-6909 mint and burn (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336) still run, so holders can trade a frozen token for another token inside the PoolManager while other reserves last. The severity stays high under the scale: a token issuer or policy admin must act, and the whole balance of the token is in reach.

findings.title: A pause of the USDC token on Arc stops the ERC-20 face and leaves native transfers open over the same PoolManager balance
findings.difference: The pause flag of USDC on Arc lives in the token contract and guards transfer, transferFrom, mint, burn and the signature-based entry points with whenNotPaused. Native value transfers are checked by the EVM against the blocklist only. On Ethereum a paused USDC has no second way to move.
findings.mechanism: 1. The pauser (0x51fa31e029abf0ce307bca9ee6bf48aed6345212) calls pause on the USDC proxy. 2. take of currency 0x3600 calls transfer and reverts with 'Pausable: paused' (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86), and no payer can move ERC-20 USDC to the PoolManager, so settle for 0x3600 credits nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). collectProtocolFees for 0x3600 reverts as well (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 3. take of address(0) still pays with a value call (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52) and settle with msg.value still works (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354). 4. Claims and pool balances are recorded per currency id, so holders of 0x3600 claims cannot leave while holders of address(0) claims on the same balance can. A pool that pairs the two faces becomes the only exit for 0x3600 holders, at whatever price that pool reaches.
findings.impact: Every pool and claim denominated in 0x3600 is frozen for the length of the pause. At block 32,584,426 the PoolManager held 2,445,327.82 USDC in total for both faces. I did not split that figure between the two ids. Native-denominated pools keep working.
findings.preconditions: The USDC pauser, a Circle role, must pause the token. An ordinary account cannot reach this path. The asymmetry was reproduced with eth_call and a state override of the paused bit and no transaction was sent.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers who want an exit during a token pause can hold USDC positions under address(0). Interfaces should state which face a pool uses.
