findings.title: Issuer block lists on USDC, USDT0, PYUSD and cbBTC cover the single PoolManager address on Arbitrum One
findings.difference: This is the same issuer power that exists on Ethereum, and cycle 1 did not record it for Arbitrum One. Native USDC, USDT0, PYUSD and cbBTC on Arbitrum One each have a role that can block an address, and USDT0 has an owner function that destroys the balance of a blocked address. The PoolManager holds every pool's balance of each token at one address.
findings.mechanism: Step 1: the role holder lists the PoolManager address. Step 2: the token's transfer then fails when the PoolManager is the sender. Currency.transfer reverts on a failed call, so every take and every protocol fee collection in that token reverts. Where the token also rejects a listed recipient, a settle cannot be funded either. I did not test which of the four tokens check the recipient. Step 3: liquidity providers can still remove liquidity and keep the blocked side as ERC-6909 claims through mint, which moves no tokens, but the claims cannot be turned into tokens while the block stands. Step 4, USDT0 only: the owner calls destroyBlockedFunds for the PoolManager, which lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) with no matching delta. Pool reserves, claims and accrued fees then exceed the balance and the last withdrawers bear the shortfall.
findings.impact: All pools and claims in the listed token. At the time of the queries the PoolManager held 8.99M USDC, 0.98M USDT0, 28,236 PYUSD and 14.8 cbBTC.
findings.preconditions: The blacklister of USDC (0xac5b4946a8c29eafb42e1742b3ab82e6d5771329), the owner of USDT0 (0x4dff9b5b0143e642a3f63a5bcf2d1c328e600bf8), the PYUSD role holder or the cbBTC blacklister must act. All four tokens report the PoolManager as not blocked today. An arbitrary caller is rejected by each of these functions.
findings.mitigations: None in the PoolManager. Liquidity providers can watch the block list views for the PoolManager address. A blocked side can be held as claims until the block is lifted.

USDC returns blacklister() 0xac5b4946a8c29eafb42e1742b3ab82e6d5771329 and isBlacklisted(PoolManager) false, and blacklist(PoolManager) from an arbitrary sender reverts with 'Blacklistable: caller is not the blacklister'. USDC therefore blocks both directions, which the finding left untested. USDT0 returns owner() 0x4dff9b5b0143e642a3f63a5bcf2d1c328e600bf8 and isBlocked(PoolManager) false, and addToBlockedList and destroyBlockedFunds revert for an arbitrary sender with 'Ownable: caller is not the owner'. In a simulation the owner blocks the PoolManager, a transfer from the PoolManager reverts with 'TetherToken: from is blocked', destroyBlockedFunds succeeds and balanceOf(PoolManager) reads zero afterwards. PYUSD returns isFrozen(PoolManager) false and freeze from an arbitrary sender reverts with a missing role error. cbBTC returns blacklister() 0x2b1565cd8bf6b5126cedb5000bc2d855bcbcedb8 and isBlacklisted(PoolManager) false. Balances at the PoolManager were 8.80M USDC, 0.96M USDT0, 25,779 PYUSD and 15.11 cbBTC. I did not simulate a freeze on PYUSD or cbBTC.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller and then calls Currency.transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For an ERC-20 the call result must be success with empty return data or a 32 byte value of 1, and anything else reverts with a wrapped ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-56). A blocked PoolManager therefore cannot pay out the token through any path. mint lowers the caller's delta and writes an ERC-6909 balance without calling the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329, src/ERC6909.sol:79-83), so a provider can still remove liquidity and hold the blocked side as claims. _settle credits only a measured rise in balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), so when the token also rejects the PoolManager as recipient no debt in that token can be paid and swaps that pay it in revert. A burn of the PoolManager balance by the issuer lowers balanceOf with no delta, and nothing in the code reduces pool amounts, claims or accrued fees to match.
verification.corrections: The balances moved since the research queries. For USDC the block applies to transfers in both directions. The actor and the severity stand: only the role holders can act, and the scale puts a freeze that needs a token issuer at high.

findings.title: X Layer voids blacklisted L1 deposits at the execution layer, so forced inclusion is no guaranteed exit from the PoolManager
findings.difference: On Ethereum nobody can stop a valid transaction from executing once it is in a block. On a standard OP Stack chain a deposit sent through the OptimismPortal on Ethereum must be executed on L2 as written, which gives users an exit that the sequencer cannot refuse. The X Layer execution client adds a consensus rule: before it runs a user deposit it asks the TxBlacklist contract at 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 whether the deposit's source hash is listed, and a listed deposit is recorded as a failed deposit without running its call. The contract is an upgradeable proxy. Its owner and the owner of its proxy admin are one account without code, 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa.
findings.mechanism: 1. Every pool's funds leave the PoolManager through take inside unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 291-297), and a liquidity position belongs to the msg.sender that created it (src/PoolManager.sol:159-167). An exit is therefore a transaction that must execute on X Layer from the position owner's address. 2. Cycle 1 recorded that the X Layer block builder can leave out sequencer submitted transactions through a risk control filter, and that an L1 deposit remained as the exit. 3. In the client source at tag xlayer/v0.1.7, OpEvm::transact_raw calls intercept_blacklisted_deposit before it executes a transaction. For a deposit that is not a system transaction and does not come from the L1 attributes depositor, it makes an uncommitted system call isBlacklisted(sourceHash) from 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe to the address that the source fixes for chain id 196. 4. When the call returns true, the client builds the result through the handler's failed deposit path: every change of the transaction is reverted, the sender nonce is bumped, the mint is kept and the call to the target is never made. The deposit is included in the block and has no effect. 5. A source hash is known from the moment the deposit event is emitted on Ethereum. User deposits are executed in the first L2 block of the epoch whose origin is that Ethereum block, and the sequencer builds this block after the Ethereum block exists and may lag behind it inside the sequencing window. The party that controls the blacklist therefore has time to list the hash before the deposit is executed. 6. On chain, addToBlacklist(bytes32) reverts for an arbitrary sender, for the owner and for the PoolManager. The implementation has an operators(address) mapping and the setOperator(address,bool) selector, so the owner appoints the accounts that can list hashes. The same owner can replace the implementation through the proxy admin. 7. A liquidity provider whose ordinary transactions are filtered by the builder and whose deposits are listed has no remaining way to call the PoolManager. The code in src/ has no path that works without transaction execution.
findings.impact: Funds of any chosen liquidity provider, swapper or claim holder on X Layer can be held in the PoolManager for as long as the operator keeps filtering and listing. This covers 307.9 OKB and 5,889,016 USDT0 at the time of the query. Nothing is taken: the code has no time dependence, so the funds are intact when the block is lifted. The rule is part of the state transition that every X Layer node applies. The release notes say the same Rust stack is used for proof generation, so a proof would be expected to accept a voided deposit as correct. I did not read the proof program to confirm this.
findings.preconditions: The holder of 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, or an operator that this account appoints, must list each deposit's source hash before the deposit is executed, and the sequencer must also keep the same user's ordinary transactions out of blocks. An ordinary account cannot list a hash. Whether any hash has been listed could not be read, because the public endpoint limits log queries to 100 blocks. The tag xlayer/v0.1.7 is the op-node release that operators had to run by 10 November 2026. The exact submodule commit that the mainnet sequencer runs was not confirmed, and the blacklist file is also present at tag xlayer/v0.1.6.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should treat X Layer positions as dependent on one operator account and should not rely on L1 forced inclusion as an exit. The deployer can ask OKX to publish the conditions under which deposits are listed and to move ownership of the blacklist and its proxy admin to a multisignature account with a delay. Integrators can monitor the blacklist contract for operator changes and new entries.

User deposited transactions are placed in the first L2 block of an epoch and are derived from the receipts of the L1 origin block. An L2 block timestamp is at or after the timestamp of its L1 origin, and the L2 blocks of an epoch are derived from the sequencing window that starts at that origin.
The block builder screens each transaction against rules from an external risk control service and excludes transactions with a deny verdict.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the three client files at tag xlayer/v0.1.7 of okx/optimism. xlayer_blacklist_contract.rs maps chain id 196 to 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727, calls isBlacklisted(sourceHash) through transact_system_call from the EIP-4788 system address, treats a revert or a malformed answer as false, and exempts system deposits and the L1 attributes depositor. In lib.rs, transact_raw calls intercept_blacklisted_deposit for every transaction, with no fork or flag condition. The function returns early for anything that is not a user deposit, and on a hit it passes an InvalidTransaction error with the text 'deposit blacklisted' to OpHandler::catch_error and returns the finalized state. In op-revm handler.rs, catch_error for a deposit reverts to the first journal checkpoint, bumps the caller nonce, adds the mint and commits. The same two files are present with the same mainnet address at the okx/optimism ref xlayer-dep/a492b62bbecbdcf3be90719e042c9abca47c8cc6 and on main. The release page for xlayer/v0.1.6 lists 'feat(rcs): intercept blacklisted L1 deposits before execution (51ce81a)' and says that release was for testnet only. The release pages for xlayer/v0.1.7 and xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3 say operators must run both by November 10, 2026, and neither page names the blacklist. Cargo.toml of xlayer-reth at tag v0.0.7.3 takes alloy-op-evm and op-revm from the path deps/optimism/rust, and .gitmodules points that path at okx/optimism. On chain at X Layer block 76,601,162 on 2026-11-22: the endpoint reports reth/v2.3.0-f60420a with the suffix xlayer/v0.0.7. The blacklist address holds 1,059 bytes of code, its EIP-1967 implementation slot holds 0xe44bfef30cfd8ecbfb917d78fa2ac215b3397f8e (3,516 bytes) and its admin slot holds 0x57ffb399eb2d8fb1831001ba893483bc13bd8c2f. owner() on the proxy and on the admin both return 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, which has no code and account nonce 2,098. pendingOwner() is zero. The implementation bytecode contains the selectors of isBlacklisted(bytes32), blacklisted(bytes32), addToBlacklist(bytes32), removeFromBlacklist(bytes32), batchAddToBlacklist(bytes32[]), batchRemoveFromBlacklist(bytes32[]), operators(address) and setOperator(address,bool). addToBlacklist reverts with 0x7c214f04, the selector of NotOperator(), for an arbitrary sender and for the owner. setOperator(address,bool) succeeds in simulation from the owner and reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount for another sender. isBlacklisted returns false for a test hash when called from 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe. eth_getLogs for the contract over the last 100 blocks returned nothing. The OP Stack derivation specification says user deposits are placed in the first L2 block of an epoch, before sequenced transactions, and that an L2 block may keep an L1 origin whose timestamp is up to max_sequencer_drift older than its own. A hash therefore has to be listed in an L2 block that precedes the block of the deposit, and the sequencer chooses when it advances to the L1 origin that holds the deposit. One link is backed by release documents and not by direct observation: I could not read the submodule pointer of xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3, and I found no deposit that was voided on mainnet.
verification.codeCheck: Funds leave the PoolManager through take, which carries onlyWhenUnlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 96-99), and unlock hands control to msg.sender and requires all deltas to be zero on return (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). A liquidity position is stored under msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161), so only that account can reduce it. ERC-6909 claims are burned from an account by that account, by its operator or by a spender with allowance (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22), and each of these still needs a transaction on X Layer. collectProtocolFees pays out accrued protocol fees only and needs the controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). No function in src/ depends on block time or lets a third party withdraw for an owner without the owner's earlier approval. A user whose transactions are never executed therefore cannot move funds out. I found no guard in src/ that the finding missed, and none could exist, because the hazard sits below the contract.
verification.corrections: The actor value operator is right: an ordinary account cannot list a hash and cannot make the sequencer filter a transaction. The balances moved since the research query. The PoolManager held 300.77 OKB and 5,945,282 USDT0 at block 76,601,162. Step 7 of the mechanism holds only while every transaction that could move the position is stopped. An account that already holds an ERC-6909 operator approval, an allowance or a PositionManager approval from the owner can act for the owner from a different sender, and the operator would have to filter or list that transaction as well. The finding says the rule is active by construction for chain id 196. That statement is true of the source at the release tag. Whether the running sequencer build pins that commit is unconfirmed, as the finding itself notes. Severity high follows the scale, since a freeze needs a privileged chain-level actor, and it matches the Robinhood Chain filter finding F-001.

findings.title: A Stylus program used as a hook or token stops answering calls on expiry or a Stylus version change, and activation is blocked
findings.difference: On Ethereum, code at an address keeps answering calls. On Arbitrum One a contract can be a Stylus WASM program. A call to it fails unless the program was activated at the current Stylus version and its last activation or keepalive is less than 365 days old. ArbOS 61, active since 2026-08-20, moved the Stylus version from 2 to 3. On chain, ArbWasm.activationGas() is 2^64-1, which makes activateProgram fail for everyone, so a program that has expired or needs the new version cannot be brought back by its users.
findings.mechanism: Hook path: the PoolManager calls the hook with call() and reverts the whole action when the call fails. For a hook address with the before or after remove liquidity flag, modifyLiquidity with a negative delta calls the hook, so a hook that no longer answers blocks every liquidity removal in its pools. Hooks with swap or donate flags block those actions the same way. Token path: transfer and balanceOf on a Stylus token that no longer answers revert, so take, sync and settle revert for that currency in every pool. Step 1: a pool is created with a Stylus hook or a Stylus token while the program is active. Step 2: the program reaches 365 days without a keepalive, or an ArbOS upgrade changes the Stylus version. getActiveProgram returns ProgramExpired or ProgramNeedsUpgrade and the call fails. Step 3: anyone who tries activateProgram is charged activationGas first, which exceeds any gas limit, so the call fails. Keepalive works only while the program is still active and at least 31 days old. ArbOS 61 also removed WASM multi-value support, so a program that relies on it cannot be reactivated even when activation reopens. I did not enumerate which pools on Arbitrum One use a Stylus hook or token, and I did not establish the date on which activation gas was raised, so I cannot say how many programs missed the move to version 3.
findings.impact: LP principal and fees in pools whose hook gates liquidity removal are stuck for as long as activation stays closed. For a Stylus token, every balance of that token in the PoolManager is stuck. No funds move to an attacker. Pools without Stylus hooks or tokens are unaffected.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use a Stylus program as its hook or as one of its currencies. Then either nobody pays for keepalive within the 365 day window, or governance ships a Stylus version change. No attacker action is required and none can speed it up. The Arbitrum Foundation or Security Council can reopen activation.
findings.mitigations: Pool creators on Arbitrum One should prefer EVM hooks. LPs in a pool with a Stylus hook should check ArbWasm.programVersion and programTimeLeft for the hook and for each token, and anyone can pay codehashKeepalive once the program is 31 days old. A hook author can leave the remove liquidity flags unset so that removals never depend on the hook.

sources.supports: CallProgram calls getActiveProgram, which returns an error when the program version differs from the Stylus version or the program is older than ExpiryDays. ProgramKeepalive requires an active program at least KeepaliveDays old.
The ArbOS 59 upgrade step calls UpgradeToVersion(3) on the Stylus parameters.
ActivateProgram burns the configurable activation gas before activation. CodehashKeepalive does not.

sources.url: https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc eth_call ArbWasm.activationGas(), stylusVersion(), expiryDays(), keepaliveDays() at 0x71; queried 2026-11-22
sources.supports: activationGas is 0xffffffffffffffff, the Stylus version is 3, expiry is 365 days and keepalive needs 31 days.
New activations and reactivation of expired programs are paused on Arbitrum One. Active programs run until they expire and can be renewed with keepalive.
ArbOS 61 activated on Arbitrum One on 2026-08-20 and programs that rely on WASM multi-value can no longer be activated or reactivated.
Stylus contracts must be reactivated once per 365 days or after any Stylus upgrade, and otherwise become uncallable.
The proposal to reopen activation through an Arbitrum Foundation process was put on hold on 2026-11-18, and a later ArbOS proposal plans the ability to deactivate a Stylus contract.

verification.factCheck: I read arbos/programs/programs.go at Nitro v3.11.3. CallProgram calls getActiveProgram, which returns ProgramNeedsUpgrade when the program version differs from the Stylus version and ProgramExpired when the age exceeds ExpiryDays. ProgramKeepalive needs an active program that is at least KeepaliveDays old. I read arbos/arbosState/arbosstate.go and arbos/programs/params.go. The ArbOS 59 step calls UpgradeToVersion(3), which sets the Stylus version from 2 to 3. I read precompiles/ArbWasm.go. ActivateProgram burns the stored activation gas first. CodehashKeepalive does not. On chain at Arbitrum One block 526,514,058 on 2026-11-22: stylusVersion() is 3, expiryDays() is 365, keepaliveDays() is 31 and activationGas() is 2^64-1. A simulated activateProgram with 30,000,000 gas reverts. I tested the effect directly. ProgramActivated logs of ArbWasm around block 496,578,581, the first block at or after the ArbOS 61 activation time, show version 2 before it and version 3 after it. The program 0x2e5d89a229cbd17efb0a731d26232f88c3746aa9, activated at version 2 in block 495,363,914 and not reactivated, now fails every eth_call with the error ProgramNeedsUpgrade(2, 3). The program 0xaff2f129d2bcba4649a54fb516be0cc78288898d was reactivated at version 3 in block 496,871,745 and answers calls. The finding did not establish when activation was closed. The Security Council report gives the date: on 2026-10-02 the council called ArbOwner.setWasmActivationGas(2^64 - 1) on Arbitrum One and Nova. ArbOS 61 activated on 2026-08-20 at 17:00 UTC, so programs had 43 days to move to version 3. The pause notice, the ArbOS 61 release notes, the Stylus introduction and the forum proposal say what the finding reports. The last post of the forum thread, by the authors on 2026-11-18, says they will integrate feedback before taking the proposal further, and the first post says protocol-level activation controls and the ability to deactivate a Stylus contract are planned for a later ArbOS proposal. I also measured exposure. The PoolManager on Arbitrum One emitted 28,689 Initialize events from block 290,000,000 to block 526,516,712, with 923 distinct hook addresses and 9,417 distinct currency addresses. None of them has code that starts with the Stylus prefix 0xeff0. No pool therefore has a Stylus program as its direct hook or currency today. This check reads the code at the hook or token address only. It does not see an EVM contract that forwards to a Stylus program.
verification.codeCheck: callHook makes a plain call with all gas and reverts with HookCallFailed when the call fails. A call that succeeds with fewer than 32 bytes also reverts with InvalidHookResponse (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). For a negative or zero liquidityDelta, beforeModifyLiquidity calls the hook when the address has the before remove liquidity flag, and afterModifyLiquidity does so for the after remove liquidity flag (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-206, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:209-245). Both run inside modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:156, src/PoolManager.sol:178). The only bypass is noSelfCall, which skips the hook when the hook itself is the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:217). A program that cannot run cannot be the caller. Permissions come from the address bits (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:337-339) and the hook address is part of the pool identifier, so an LP cannot route around it. For a token, balanceOfSelf is a high-level call that reverts when the call fails (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96), and transfer reverts with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:54-87). sync, the ERC-20 branch of _settle and take all revert for that currency (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). Claims in that currency can still be minted, burned and transferred. test/PoolManager.t.sol and test/DynamicFees.t.sol cover a hook that reverts or returns a bad response. No test covers a hook or token whose code stops answering after pool creation.
verification.corrections: The mechanism and the chain facts hold. The scope needs two changes. First, no pool on Arbitrum One has a Stylus program as its direct hook or currency today, so no funds are frozen through the direct path at present. Indirect use through an EVM proxy or an EVM hook that calls a Stylus program was not checked. Second, the date the finding could not establish is 2026-10-02, 43 days after the version change. The same mechanism reaches Robinhood Chain. Its ArbWasm precompile emitted 26 ProgramActivated events between 2026-07-25 and 2026-10-02, all at version 3, and activation gas there is also 2^64-1. Those programs expire from 2027-07-25 unless someone pays keepalive, and a Stylus version change would stop them at once. On Robinhood Chain the PoolManager emitted 1,169,661 Initialize events up to block 120.6M. 411,764 of them name a hook, across 32,935 distinct hook addresses and 745,518 distinct currency addresses. None of the 26 activated program addresses is a hook or a currency of any pool. I read the code of the 1,500 most used hook addresses, which cover 377,624 of the hooked pools, and none starts with 0xeff0. I did not read the code of the remaining hooks or of the currencies, so a contract that shares its code hash with an activated program is not excluded there. The severity stays medium because the freeze is limited to pools that depend on a Stylus program and needs either a missed keepalive or a governance upgrade.

findings.title: A pool's hook can block or reprice every liquidity removal in that pool, and core has no path that skips the hook
findings.difference: None. The code path is the same on every network. Networks where the code behind an address can change after pool creation (A7) add ways for a hook that was harmless at creation to start doing this.
findings.mechanism: modifyLiquidity calls the hook library's beforeModifyLiquidity before it touches the pool (src/PoolManager.sol:156). For liquidityDelta <= 0 the library calls beforeRemoveLiquidity when address bit 9 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204). callHook reverts the whole call when the hook reverts (Hooks.sol:134-137) and when the return data is shorter than 32 bytes or carries the wrong selector (Hooks.sol:152-154). A hook address with no code returns empty data, so it also reverts. After the pool update, afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set, and when bit 0 is also set it reads a BalanceDelta from the return data, subtracts it from the caller's delta without any bound and credits it to the hook (Hooks.sol:232-243, src/PoolManager.sol:177-183). The hook call is skipped only when msg.sender is the hook itself (Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). No other function removes liquidity. The swap path has the same shape: beforeSwap and afterSwap deltas move value between swapper and hook (Hooks.sol:248-315), and the hook of a dynamic fee pool can set the LP fee to 100 percent (src/PoolManager.sol:339-346, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:25, 37-45).
findings.impact: Principal and uncollected fees of every position in the affected pool. A reverting hook freezes them. A hook with the return delta bit can take part or all of what a removal would pay out, up to what the LP's router accepts. Funds in other pools are not reachable this way, because the caller delta plus the hook delta always equals the pool delta (Hooks.sol:230, 242, 312) and each party must net to zero before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112).
findings.preconditions: The pool's hook address has bit 9 (0x200) or bit 8 (0x100) set, and for taking funds also bit 0. The hook code reverts, returns a bad selector, returns a hostile delta, or is replaced or removed after LPs deposit. LPs must have chosen that pool. This is how the hook design works; I list it because it is a path to a freeze or loss that the text of core does not limit.
findings.mitigations: LPs and position managers can read the low 14 bits of the hook address before depositing and treat bits 9, 8 and 0 as custody risk unless the hook code is immutable and reviewed. Routers should enforce minimum amounts on removal so a hostile return delta reverts. The deployer cannot change this without adding a removal path that skips hooks.

verification.factCheck: The finding claims no network difference, so the chain facts to check are its remark that code behind a hook address can change after pool creation and whether the repository expects the behaviour. I fetched EIP-7702, status Final. It says each authorization writes the delegation indicator 0xef0100 || address into the authorizing account's code, that a later authorization can point elsewhere or clear the code, and that code executing operations load the code the delegation points to. An externally owned account whose low 14 bits carry hook flags can therefore act as a hook, and its owner can replace or remove the logic later. I fetched EIP-6780, which limits account deletion by SELFDESTRUCT to the transaction that created the contract. On chain, eth_getCode on Arbitrum One for 0xa853180523bd16fa6a9c449ab050e108da642488 returned 0xef01001947e2c7b5ca44f2db6236cf5ac3e23457e8a488, which is a delegation indicator at an address whose low bits set beforeInitialize, afterAddLiquidity, beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnsDelta. I did not confirm that an initialized pool uses that address, and it does not carry the removal bits 9 or 8. The repository's own tests expect the behaviour the finding describes. test/PoolManager.t.sol:272-287 expects a removal to revert with InvalidHookResponse when the hook returns a wrong selector. test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:297-322 expects a hook to receive 5.43 percent of a withdrawal through the afterRemoveLiquidity return delta.
verification.codeCheck: modifyLiquidity is the only function that changes a position (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184). It calls beforeModifyLiquidity before the pool update (src/PoolManager.sol:156). For liquidityDelta <= 0 with bit 9 set the library calls beforeRemoveLiquidity (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204). callHook reverts when the call fails (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134-137) and when the return data is shorter than 32 bytes or the selector differs (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154). A call to an address without code succeeds with empty return data and then fails the length check. After the pool update, afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:233-241), requires exactly 64 bytes of return data when bit 0 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:166) and subtracts the returned delta from the caller's delta (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:242). The subtraction is bounded only by the int128 range (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:34-46). The hook delta is credited to the hook address and the remainder to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:181-183). The only bypass is a call where msg.sender is the hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). I looked for a guard the finding missed and found none: there is no removal path without the hook call and no cap on the return delta. The caller delta and the hook delta always sum to the pool delta, and unlock reverts unless every delta is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112), so funds of other pools are out of reach, and a return delta larger than the payout succeeds only when the LP's own unlock callback pays the shortfall. The swap path matches the description (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:248-315), and updateDynamicLPFee accepts any fee up to 1,000,000 from the hook of a dynamic fee pool (src/PoolManager.sol:339-346, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:25, 37-45).
verification.corrections: The difference field presents changing code as a property of some networks. EIP-7702 delegation and upgradeable proxy hooks make it possible on every network that has activated EIP-7702, Ethereum included, so the exposure does not depend on the network. The freeze case needs nothing from the LP. The taking case needs the LP's router to accept the reduced amount, as the finding says. The add liquidity path has the same shape through bits 11, 10 and 1, which can block or surcharge deposits and cannot hold existing funds. Severity stays medium because the loss is limited to pools whose LPs chose that hook address, and the tests show this is the intended trust model.

findings.title: Uncollected fees above the int128 maximum make every later update of a liquidity position revert
findings.difference: None. The condition is the same on every network. It needs a token whose supply in base units is larger than 2^127 - 1, about 1.7e38. The comment at src/libraries/Pool.sol:403 says the code assumes token supply stays within uint128.
findings.mechanism: Every modifyLiquidity call, including a zero delta poke and a removal, runs Position.update and then casts both fee amounts with feesOwed0.toInt128() and feesOwed1.toInt128() (src/libraries/Pool.sol:184-192). Position.update computes the fee as (feeGrowthInside - feeGrowthInsideLast) * liquidity / 2^128 for the whole position (src/libraries/Position.sol:92-97). SafeCast.toInt128(uint256) reverts for values of 2^127 or more (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). Because the whole call reverts, the position's fee checkpoint is never updated. The amount owed therefore never goes down, and every later call for that position reverts the same way, whatever liquidityDelta is used. Fees reach a position through swaps (Pool.sol:401-407) and through donate (Pool.sol:466-480). Each single donate or swap is capped at int128, so the threshold is crossed over two or more calls. I confirmed the arithmetic with a Python transcription of Pool, Position and SafeCast: after two donations of 2^126 + 10 units to a range with one position, updates with delta 0, -1, -1e18 and +1 all revert.
findings.impact: The principal in both currencies and the uncollected fees of that one position stay in the PoolManager with no way out. Other positions in the pool and other pools are not affected.
findings.preconditions: One position must be owed 2^127 base units or more of one currency in fees that it has not yet collected. Fees owed are real tokens paid by swappers or donors, so the token's supply in base units must exceed 1.7e38 and a payer must give up that amount. For a token with a supply below that bound the state cannot be reached. A party that controls such a token's supply can already drain the other side of the pool by selling, so this adds a way to freeze but no extra profit.
findings.mitigations: LPs can avoid pools with a token whose base unit supply exceeds 2^127, and can collect fees with a zero delta call before the amount owed gets near the bound. Pool creators can check totalSupply and decimals. A code change that caps or splits the fee credit would remove the condition.

verification.factCheck: The finding states no network difference and I found none, because the path uses no chain feature. No external source applies, so the facts are in the repository. I recomputed the arithmetic on my own. Two donations of 2^126 + 10 base units into a range with one position give a fee growth for which Position.update returns 2^127 + 19 or 2^127 + 20 for position liquidity of 1, 1e6, 1e18 and about 2^100. Each value is at or above the bound where SafeCast.toInt128 reverts. No test covers the case. test/PoolManager.t.sol:908-915 bounds a single donation to the int128 maximum, and test/libraries/Position.t.sol:26-70 fuzzes Position.update without the cast that follows it in Pool. Two links are unconfirmed. I could not confirm whether any token held by a deployed PoolManager has a base unit supply above 2^127 - 1, which is the researcher's open lead. I did not exercise the path on the deployed contracts, because it needs an unlock callback and a read only call cannot reach it.
verification.codeCheck: Pool.modifyLiquidity calls Position.update for every liquidityDelta, including zero and negative values, and then casts both fee amounts with toInt128 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:183-193). Position.update computes fees on the full liquidity held before the update (src/libraries/Position.sol:82, 92-97). SafeCast.toInt128(uint256) reverts at 2^127 (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). The revert undoes the checkpoint write at src/libraries/Position.sol:100-101, so the amount owed can stay or grow and cannot shrink. The ticks of a position that holds liquidity keep a nonzero liquidityGross, so their feeGrowthOutside values are set once and are cleared only when the last position leaves (src/libraries/Pool.sol:533-539, 196-203). Fee growth inside the range can therefore not be lowered by anyone. Wrapping the growth difference past 2^256 would take further real payments of roughly 2^128 times the position liquidity less the amount already owed, which for any realistic liquidity is far more than a uint128 supply. Pool.donate caps one donation below 2^127 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:471) and the casts on the swap delta cap one swap (src/libraries/Pool.sol:454-460), so the bound is crossed over two or more payments. The owed fees are backed by tokens: a donor who shares the range receives only its own pro rata share back, so the victim's share has to be paid in. There is no partial fee collection and no other exit, so the principal of that position in both currencies stays in the PoolManager.
verification.corrections: Severity raised from low to medium. The scale reserves low for hazards with no direct loss path, and this is a direct and permanent freeze of a position, limited to pools with a token whose base unit supply exceeds 2^127 - 1. The actor is any holder of 2^127 base units who gives them up as a donation or as swap fees, or ordinary swap volume against a passive position that never collects. The bound is 2^127, half of the uint128 supply that the comment at src/libraries/Pool.sol:403 names as the assumption, so a token inside the stated assumption with a supply between 2^127 and 2^128 can still reach it. The finding's point that an issuer with unlimited supply can already empty the pool by selling holds, and it does not cover a third party token with a large fixed supply, where the attacker gains nothing and the LP still loses access to both currencies of the position.

findings.title: Scheduled Jenner fork adds protocol-native tokens whose issuer can seize, pause or block the PoolManager balance
findings.difference: BNB Smart Chain has scheduled the Jenner fork for 2026-12-08 02:30 UTC. It ships BEP-702, a token standard named CAS20 that runs as native code behind addresses starting with 0xCA52. Every CAS20 token has a role that can reassign a holder's balance (seizeWithMemo), a per-feature pause, and transfer policies that read shared allowlists and blocklists. BEP-703 lets governance list these tokens as payment assets with reserved block space. Ethereum has no token logic in the protocol.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager keeps every pool's reserves, all ERC-6909 claims and accrued protocol fees for a currency in one balance, read by balanceOf at src/types/Currency.sol:94 and paid out by transfer at src/types/Currency.sol:60-75. 2. A CAS20 token keeps the transfer and balanceOf selectors, so pools can be initialized with it. initialize makes no call to the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). 3. The token admin points SEIZE_HOLDER_POLICY at a blocklist that contains the PoolManager address. An account with SEIZE_ROLE then calls seizeWithMemo(PoolManager, to, value). The balance moves without any take, and no delta is recorded. Pool accounting still shows the old reserves, so the last liquidity providers and claim holders to exit find transfer failing for lack of balance. 4. If TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY stops authorizing the PoolManager, or the TRANSFER feature is paused, the token reverts every transfer from the PoolManager. Currency.transfer then reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, so take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56) fail for every pool that uses the token. 5. If TRANSFER_RECEIVER_POLICY stops authorizing the PoolManager, nobody can pay the token in, and settle credits nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). 6. The Asset variant multiplier does not change balanceOf, so it creates no rebase at the PoolManager. That part was checked and is safe.
findings.impact: All reserves, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees held in the affected CAS20 token across every pool. Seizure is a loss for liquidity providers of those pools. A policy change or pause is a freeze that lasts until the issuer reverses it. Liquidity providers can still remove liquidity, take the counter-asset and hold the affected token as an ERC-6909 claim through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), because mint makes no token call.
findings.preconditions: Jenner activates as scheduled, chain governance opens CAS20 creation through the ActivationRegistry, a CAS20 token is created, and pools holding it exist on the PoolManager. The issuer roles of that token must then act. An unprivileged attacker can do this only with a token it issued itself, which harms only those who pool against that token. None of these conditions hold today. The factory and registry addresses have no code at the time of the query. The BEP is still marked Draft and the client implementation was not read, so the final behaviour could differ from the text.
findings.mitigations: Treat CAS20 tokens as issuer-controlled assets in interfaces and routing. Before listing a CAS20 pool, read the token's six policy ids, its pause mask and the holders of SEIZE_ROLE and the admin role. Prefer tokens whose role membership is frozen with no seizer. Liquidity providers should size positions on the assumption that the issuer can take or freeze the pooled balance. After the fork, re-test take and settle against a CAS20 token on a fork node.

verification.factCheck: BEP-702 was fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com. Its status is Draft and it was created on 2026-07-16. Section 3.3 reserves every address that starts with 0xCA52 followed by eight zero bytes. Section 3.6 says seizeWithMemo reassigns the balance of the from account without an allowance and without the transfer policies, and that the account is seizable only when the holder policy does not authorize it. Section 3.8 lists six policy scopes and says each starts at policy 0 (ALWAYS_ALLOW), so no account is seizable on an unconfigured token. Section 3.9 says pause(TRANSFER) halts transfers and leaves seizeWithMemo callable. Section 3.12 says balanceOf returns the raw balance. BEP-718 lists BEP-702, BEP-703 and BEP-706 for Jenner and says token creation is opened by a governance-appointed activation switch. The BSC CHANGELOG entry for v1.8.2 schedules mainnet Jenner for 2026-12-08 02:30:00 UTC (1796697000), and params/config.go on master sets the mainnet JennerTime to 1796697000. BEP-703 names BEP-702 native tokens as eligible payment contracts. I also read the client, which the finding did not. core/vm/evm.go on master resolves any address with the CAS20 prefix to native code once IsJenner is true. core/vm/cas20_token.go implements transfer: it reverts with ContractPaused when TRANSFER is paused, reverts with PolicyForbids when the sender policy or the receiver policy does not authorize the account, and returns a 32 byte true on success. core/vm/cas20_admin.go implements seizeWithMemo: it requires SEIZE_ROLE, skips the transfer policies and moves the balance when the seize policy does not authorize the holder. On chain at BSC block 135,080,406 on 2026-11-22: the block timestamp is 1795351088, which is 15.6 days before JennerTime, and eth_getCode is empty at 0xCA5F000000000000000000000000000000000000, 0x7020000000000000000000000000000000000001, 0x7020000000000000000000000000000000000002, 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000002007 and two addresses in the token range. Not confirmed: mainnet behaviour after activation, whether governance opens token creation, and which tokens will have pools. These lie in the future.
verification.codeCheck: sync reads balanceOf through a static call (src/PoolManager.sol:285, src/types/Currency.sol:94), and BEP-702 section 3.2 permits reads under STATICCALL. take records the debit and then calls transfer with the PoolManager as caller (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). A revert from the token reaches src/types/Currency.sol:82-86 and reverts the take. collectProtocolFees ends in the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). A CAS20 transfer returns 32 bytes holding 1, which passes the success test at src/types/Currency.sol:68. initialize makes no call to either currency (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142), so a pool can be created for any CAS20 address. A seizure lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) and writes no delta. No function in src/ reconciles pool accounting with the real balance, so takes fail with InsufficientBalance once the sum requested exceeds what is left. A seizure that lands between sync and settle makes the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 revert for that settle. With the receiver policy closed, no token can reach the PoolManager and settle credits zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). mint and burn make no token call (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336) and modifyLiquidity makes none (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184), so liquidity providers can leave with the counter-asset and an ERC-6909 claim on the frozen token, as the finding says. I found no guard in src/ that the finding missed. No test in test/ models a token whose issuer can move or block the PoolManager balance.
verification.corrections: 1. The client on master names the holder scope SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY (core/vm/cas20_admin.go), while the BEP text names it SEIZE_HOLDER_POLICY. The semantics are the same. Tools that watch the PoolManager's seizability must use the getter the client exposes. 2. The finding attributes the hazard to issuer roles only. BEP-702 section 3.8 makes the PolicyRegistry a shared singleton, so the admin of a policy list can change the PoolManager's status for every token that references the list without holding a role on any of them. 3. The finding says the client implementation was not read. It is on bnb-chain/bsc master and agrees with the BEP on transfer, pause, policy checks and seizure. 4. Severity stays medium. The actor is a token issuer, which the scale places at high. No CAS20 token exists today, the PoolManager holds none, and the loss is limited to pools of the affected token. Raise it to high once a CAS20 token with a seizer or a restrictive sender policy has a balance at the PoolManager.

findings.title: EIP-7702 lets the code behind a hook address be replaced or removed after a pool is created
findings.difference: Since Pectra (EIP-7702) an EOA can point its code at any contract through a delegation indicator, repoint it in a later transaction, or clear it. Since Dencun (EIP-6780) an ordinary contract cannot delete its code after the creation transaction. On mainnet today a delegated EOA is therefore the one kind of account whose code can change or vanish at a fixed address without a proxy pattern in its bytecode.
findings.mechanism: initialize accepts a hook address on its low 14 bits alone and never looks at code (src/PoolManager.sol:126, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127). An EOA whose address ends in chosen flag bits is cheap to find because only 14 bits must match. While the EOA delegates to honest hook code the pool behaves normally. If the account holder clears the delegation, a call to the hook succeeds with empty return data, and callHook reverts with InvalidHookResponse because the result is shorter than 32 bytes (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). With the before or after remove liquidity flag set, every liquidity removal by anyone other than the hook address then reverts (src/PoolManager.sol:156, 178; src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-206, 232-243), so LPs cannot withdraw until the holder delegates again. If the holder repoints the delegation to hostile code and the address carries a returns-delta flag, the new code can assign itself part of each withdrawal or swap, because the hook delta is credited to the hook and subtracted from the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:233-243, 298-313; src/PoolManager.sol:181-183, 224-226). The hook address is skipped when it is itself the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217, 253, 293), and a delegated EOA can originate transactions. The holder can therefore delegate to code that answers the unlock callback for its own calls and returns invalid data to hook calls made for everyone else.
findings.impact: Funds of LPs and swappers in pools that use such a hook. Other pools are not affected because pool math never reads another pool's state. The same outcome is already possible with an upgradeable proxy hook; the change is that inspecting the code at the hook address at one point in time no longer shows it.
findings.preconditions: The attacker creates the pool with a delegated EOA as hook and LPs deposit into it. I did not scan mainnet for existing pools whose hook is a delegated account.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces, routers and LPs can read the code at the hook address and reject hooks whose code is the 23 byte delegation indicator starting with 0xef0100, or that have no code. The deployer could add a code check in initialize, but the same account could delegate afterwards, so the check belongs in periphery and off-chain listing.

verification.factCheck: EIP-7702 says the authority's code is set to 0xef0100 || address, that an authorization naming the zero address clears the account's code, that an account whose code is a delegation indicator may originate transactions, and that the EIP breaks the invariant that tx.origin == msg.sender implies the topmost frame. EIP-7600 lists EIP-7702 in Pectra with mainnet activation timestamp 1746612311. EIP-6780 limits SELFDESTRUCT to sending the balance unless it runs in the creating transaction. On chain, block 26470977 contains type 0x4 transactions with authorization lists, for example 0x41f0ca4b5cb886c68b0409568d2c596f3e6db2219db7847d3f5f7596eb64725f, and eth_config reports fork id 0x07c9462e active since 1767747671, so set code transactions are live on mainnet. I did not read the code of a delegated account on chain, and I did not scan for pools whose hook is such an account.
verification.codeCheck: initialize accepts a hook on its flag bits alone (src/PoolManager.sol:126, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127) and never reads code. callHook treats a successful call with fewer than 32 bytes of return data as InvalidHookResponse (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134, 152-154), which is what a call to an address without code produces. beforeModifyLiquidity calls the hook for liquidityDelta <= 0 when the before remove flag is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-205) and afterModifyLiquidity does so for the after remove flag (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:233-243), so every removal by anyone other than the hook address reverts while the code is absent. The hook address itself is skipped (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). With a returns delta flag the value returned by the hook is credited to the hook and subtracted from the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:242, 298-313; src/PoolManager.sol:181-183, 221-226). Core places no bound on that value and gives a liquidity provider no path around the hook. I found no guard the finding missed. test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol covers InvalidHookResponse for short return data. No test covers hook code that changes after pool creation.
verification.corrections: I raise the severity from low to medium. The finding describes a direct loss and freeze path for funds in pools that use such a hook, which is the medium definition, and it matches the rating of the general hook finding in the core-code-accounting unit, of which this is one variant. The statement that inspecting the code no longer shows the risk is too strong. A delegated account has 23 bytes of code starting with 0xef0100 and an undelegated one has none, and either result is a visible warning for a hook address. The freeze also covers swaps and donations when the matching before or after flags are set, since those calls go through the same callHook.

findings.title: The AQAv2 treasury address that HyperCore sends unsigned transfers from has no HyperCore account, so it was named by a deployer and is a different address from the signer
findings.difference: Under AQAv2 HyperCore sends system transactions in every block that call transfer on the quote token with the treasury address or the linked contract as sender, to hold their balances in a 9 to 1 ratio. The sender never signs. The docs say that the treasury deployer designates the treasury address and that the two deployers send their authorizations from the staking accounts. The exchange API action authorizeAqav2Role has only the fields token and role.
findings.mechanism: F-020 left open whether the treasury address must be the account that signed the authorization. New reads answer part of it. The USDC treasury address 0xc20699185c15d0a2fd65779bb5d69f5b0b113c00 has no code, no HyperCore user role, no stake and no HyperCore balance, while its EVM nonce is 1,035,235 and system transactions from it still appear (block 51,957,665). By the docs the authorization is sent from a staking account that holds 500,000 HYPE, and this address has no stake, so the treasury address is a second address that the deployer named. If HyperCore accepts any address in that place, a treasury deployer of a quote token could name the PoolManager. HyperCore would then send transfer calls on that token with the PoolManager as msg.sender, which the token sees as ordinary transfers by the holder. Nothing in src can stop them, pool accounting is never reconciled with the token balance (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365), and the last withdrawals of that currency would revert in transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:55-87). I did not find out whether HyperCore asks the named address for consent, for example through a signed EVM transaction. That link stays unconfirmed.
findings.impact: All pools and claims in a quote token whose AQAv2 treasury address were set to the PoolManager. USDC is the only AQAv2 token seen so far, and the PoolManager holds 997.75 USDC.
findings.preconditions: A treasury deployer with 500,000 staked HYPE, a validator vote that activates AQAv2 for the token, and a HyperCore rule that accepts the PoolManager as treasury address without its consent. The third condition is not confirmed. An ordinary account cannot meet the first two.
findings.mitigations: Ask the Hyperliquid team how a treasury address is bound and whether it can be changed after activation. Watch eth_getSystemTxsByBlockNumber for any system transaction whose sender is the PoolManager.

findings.title: PoolManager ownership on Celo and X Layer rests on the upgradeable L2CrossDomainMessenger, and on X Layer a 2 of 3 Safe of EOAs can upgrade it
findings.difference: On Ethereum the owner is the governance timelock itself. On both chains the owner is a cross-chain account contract that accepts a call when msg.sender is the L2CrossDomainMessenger predeploy and that predeploy reports the Ethereum timelock as the cross-domain sender. The predeploy is a proxy. On Celo its admin is controlled by the alias of an L1 2 of 2 Safe of two 6 of 8 Safes. On X Layer its admin is controlled by a Safe on X Layer with threshold 2 and three EOA owners.
findings.mechanism: Whoever controls the messenger implementation can make it call the owner contract while reporting the timelock as sender. The owner contract then forwards a call to the PoolManager as owner. The only owner function in src/ is setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). The Owned base contract is missing from this checkout because lib/solmate is empty, so its ownership transfer functions could not be read. A controller chosen this way can set a protocol fee of at most 1000 pips per direction on any pool (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8 and 25-32) and can withdraw accrued protocol fees to any recipient (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). The fee is taken from swap input before the LP fee (src/libraries/Pool.sol:385-396). collectProtocolFees subtracts from protocolFeesAccrued with checked arithmetic, so it cannot pay out more than was accrued.
findings.impact: Up to 0.1 percent of swap input per direction on every pool for as long as the hostile controller stays, paid by swappers, plus any accrued protocol fees. Both are zero today because no controller is set. Pool reserves, ERC-6909 claims and LP principal are not reachable through the owner or the controller role.
findings.preconditions: On X Layer two of the three Safe owners must sign an upgrade of the messenger predeploy. On Celo both 6 of 8 Safes must sign. Uniswap governance can undo the controller change only through the same messenger.
findings.mitigations: Monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated and ProtocolFeeUpdated on both chains and Upgraded events on the messenger proxy. The 0.1 percent cap in the code bounds the loss.

verification.factCheck: On both chains owner() of the PoolManager returns 0x044aAF330d7fD6AE683EEc5c1C1d1fFf5196B6b7, which has 1,488 bytes of code with the same hash on Celo and X Layer. Its l1Owner() is 0x1a9C8182C09F50C8318d769245beA52c32BE35BC and its messenger() is 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000007. Celo Blockscout serves verified source for it: forward requires msg.sender to be the messenger and xDomainMessageSender() to equal l1Owner, then calls the target. protocolFeeController() is the zero address on both chains. The EIP-1967 admin slot of the messenger predeploy holds 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000018 on both chains and the implementation slot is set. On X Layer the ProxyAdmin owner is 0xC290be56089bCC83C6993583ce2cF51a7951D45A, a Safe with threshold 2 and three owners that have no code. On Celo the ProxyAdmin owner is 0x51a3a77bAF58FEf0309452ceacB09221E556F223, which has no code and unaliases to the Ethereum Safe 0x4092A77bAF58fef0309452cEaCb09221e556E112 with threshold 2 and two owners, each a 6 of 8 Safe. The Upgrade 19 notice describes the L2 Contract Manager as a consensus layer mechanism for predeploy upgrades. An eth_call with the CLZ opcode fails as not activated on both chains, so the Osaka rules that come with Karst are not active on either.
verification.codeCheck: setProtocolFeeController is owner only (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32) and no other function in src/ uses onlyOwner. setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees accept only the controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and 48). isValidProtocolFee caps each direction at 1,000 pips (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8 and 25-32), and Slot0 masks the stored value to 24 bits (src/types/Slot0.sol:78-86). Pool.swap takes the protocol share out of the fee the swapper paid in each step (src/libraries/Pool.sol:385-398), with the step fee computed in src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-105, so the share cannot exceed the fee paid. protocolFeesAccrued grows only in _swap (src/PoolManager.sol:238, src/ProtocolFees.sol:66-70) and collectProtocolFees subtracts with checked arithmetic before the transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). The owner and the controller reach accrued protocol fees and a levy of at most 0.1 percent per direction on later swaps. They do not reach pool reserves or ERC-6909 claims. lib/solmate is empty in this checkout, so Owned could not be read here. I tested the deployed contracts instead: an eth_call of transferOwnership(address) from the owner contract returns on both chains and the same call from another sender reverts with UNAUTHORIZED, as does setProtocolFeeController. The synced currency guard is covered by test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039.
verification.corrections: 1. Severity raised from low to medium. Low requires that no direct loss path was found. This finding has one: whoever controls the messenger can appoint a controller, add up to 0.1 percent per direction to every later swap and take what accrues. The actor is a chain level upgrade authority and the reach is capped at protocol fees. The same finding on the ETH gas OP Stack chains was set to medium in this cycle. 2. The owner role includes transferOwnership on the deployed contracts. A forged message can move ownership to another address, after which Uniswap governance cannot undo the change through the messenger. The finding says governance can undo it. 3. The guard in collectProtocolFees checks the synced currency and skips address(0). It does not check the lock state (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49). On Celo a native fee collection is therefore allowed while the CELO token is synced, which the research file already lists as a lead. 4. The same signers hold wider powers than the finding covers. On X Layer the proxy admin of the L1 OptimismPortal is owned by a Safe at the same address on Ethereum with threshold 2 and the same three owners, and the SystemConfig owner is one of those three accounts acting alone. On Celo the Security Council in the governance hotfix path is the same aliased Safe that owns the ProxyAdmin. The portal route is listed as a lead. 5. Accrued fees were checked for native CELO and the CELO token on Celo, where both are zero. Other currencies and X Layer were not checked.

findings.title: PoolManager ownership rests on an upgradeable messenger predeploy on five chains and on the portal alias on two, and a takeover reaches protocol fees only
findings.difference: On Ethereum the owner is a contract that acts directly. On OP Mainnet, Base, Zora, World Chain and Soneium the owner is a CrossChainAccount that accepts a call only when msg.sender is L2CrossDomainMessenger at 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000007 and xDomainMessageSender() equals the Ethereum timelock 0x1a9C8182C09F50C8318d769245beA52c32BE35BC. The messenger is a proxy whose admin is the ProxyAdmin predeploy, owned by an aliased L1 upgrade multisig, and since Karst predeploys are also upgraded by network upgrade deposits at fork activation. On Unichain and Ink the owner is the bare alias 0x2bad8182c09f50c8318d769245bea52c32be46cd, which only a deposit from the timelock through that chain's OptimismPortal can produce.
findings.mechanism: 1. Whoever controls the messenger implementation can make xDomainMessageSender() return the timelock address and call CrossChainAccount.forward, which then calls the PoolManager as owner. On the alias chains the same result needs a change to deposit derivation or to the portal. 2. The owner can call setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). 3. The controller can call setProtocolFee for any pool, limited to 1,000 pips per direction by isValidProtocolFee (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32), and can call collectProtocolFees to any recipient. 4. collectProtocolFees subtracts the amount from protocolFeesAccrued[currency] with checked arithmetic before the transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56), so it cannot pay out more than the fees accrued for that currency. Pool reserves and ERC-6909 claims are out of reach of the owner and the controller. 5. On OP Mainnet and Base the current controller forwards collections to a fixed token jar and lets anyone trigger collect, so the present setup does not let a caller redirect fees.
findings.impact: Accrued protocol fees, about 0.030 ETH of native fees on OP Mainnet and 0.034 ETH on Base at read time, plus whatever has accrued in ERC-20 currencies, which was not read, and up to 0.1 percent per direction of future swap volume on every pool of the chain. No LP principal. On the five chains without a controller nothing has accrued.
findings.preconditions: Control of the chain's L2 predeploy upgrade path: the aliased ProxyAdmin owner, a hard fork upgrade bundle, or a compromise of the L1 timelock itself. Each of these parties can already do more damage to bridged assets than to the PoolManager.
findings.mitigations: Uniswap governance can monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated and OwnershipTransferred events on each chain. Swappers and LPs can read the protocol fee of a pool from slot0 before trading. No code change in core is needed because the owner's reach is already capped by src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56.

ProxyAdmin.owner() is 0x6b1bae59d09fccbddb6c6cceb07b7279367c4e3b on OP Mainnet, Unichain, Ink and Soneium, 0x8cc51c3008b3f03fe483b28b8db90e19cf076a6d on Base, 0x5b5a62275df8c60a80d3a25faec5aa7de116b857 on Zora and 0xb2aa0c2c4fd6bfcbf699d4c787cd6cc0dc461a9d on World Chain. The OP docs identify 0x6b1b as the alias of the 2 of 2 Safe of the Foundation and the Security Council. The OP specification overview states that network upgrade transactions at fork activation call L2ProxyAdmin.upgradePredeploys from the depositor account, and the Upgrade 19 notice introduces that mechanism with Karst. The V4FeeAdapter source on OP Mainnet shows collect without access control sending to the immutable TOKEN_JAR. TOKEN_JAR() and POOL_MANAGER() on the OP Mainnet and Base controllers return fixed addresses and the right PoolManager. Accrued native fees are 0.0304 ETH on OP Mainnet and 0.0508 ETH on Base, and zero on the five chains with a zero controller. Accrued USDC on Base read 414 and then 14 a few minutes later, which fits a permissionless collect.
verification.codeCheck: setProtocolFeeController is owner only (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). lib/solmate is an empty submodule in this checkout, so I read Owned.sol from the pinned commit 4b47a19: onlyOwner requires msg.sender == owner, and transferOwnership is the only other owner function. A search of src/ finds no other use of onlyOwner. setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees accept only the controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and 48). The fee is capped at 1,000 pips per direction (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32). protocolFeesAccrued grows only in _swap by amountToProtocol (src/PoolManager.sol:238, src/ProtocolFees.sol:66-70), which Pool.swap takes out of the fee the swapper paid in each step (src/libraries/Pool.sol:385-398). collectProtocolFees subtracts with checked arithmetic before the transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). The owner and the controller therefore reach accrued protocol fees and a levy of at most 0.1 percent per direction on later swaps. They do not reach pool reserves or ERC-6909 claims. The only guard on collection is the synced currency check (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). It is covered by test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039, and the caller checks by test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.t.sol:42-80.
verification.corrections: 1. Severity raised from low to medium. The definition of low requires that no direct loss path was found. This finding has one: a party that controls the predeploy upgrade path or a fork bundle can appoint itself controller, take accrued fees and add up to 0.1 percent per direction to every later swap. The actor is chain governance, which would place it at high, and the reach is capped at protocol fees, so medium fits. 2. The list of actors is incomplete. Network upgrade deposits are written by the fork authors and can carry any sender. The Ecotone and Isthmus specifications define upgrade deposits sent from the zero address. A fork bundle could therefore call the PoolManager as the alias owner directly, or as the zero address controller on Unichain, Zora, World Chain, Ink and Soneium, without touching the messenger. 3. The statement that nothing has accrued on the five chains was checked for the native currency only. 4. Fee figures move: Base native fees were 0.0508 ETH at my read against 0.034 in the finding.

findings.title: stHYPE and wstHYPE are two currency ids over one share balance, so a loss in the rebasing face is paid from the shares of pools in the other face
findings.difference: The StakedHYPE liquid staking token on HyperEVM has two ERC-20 contracts that read and write the same storage. stHYPE at 0xfFaa4a3D97fE9107Cef8a3F48c069F577Ff76cC1 stores shares with 24 decimals and reports shares times totalSupply divided by totalShares. wstHYPE at 0x94e8396e0869c9F2200760aF0621aFd240E1CF38 keeps no balances: its balanceOf returns stHYPE.sharesOf divided by 1e6 and its transfer calls stHYPE.transferShares. Every holder has both balances at once, and a transfer through either contract changes both. The issuer's docs describe this and warn that multi entry point tokens have caused losses elsewhere. The stHYPE figure rises every second, because totalSupply is interpolated over an interval of 82,800 seconds, and a rebase to a lower supply applies in the same transaction. On Ethereum, stETH and wstETH are separate tokens with separate balances.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager treats the two addresses as unrelated currencies. Deltas, pool reserves and ERC-6909 claims are recorded per currency address in that currency's unit (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41, src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). A take under either id calls transfer on that contract and moves shares out of the single balance the PoolManager holds (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-87). Let S be the shares the PoolManager holds, W the amount owed under the wstHYPE id in shares, T the amount owed under the stHYPE id in stHYPE units, and r the stHYPE per share rate. The PoolManager can pay everyone while S is at least W plus T divided by r. I first checked what an ordinary account can do. A credit under either id needs a rise of that contract's balanceOf between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365). Both balances rise only when shares arrive, since r depends on block.timestamp and is constant inside one transaction (stHYPE.sol lines 495 to 513) and Overseer.rebase reverts for a caller without REBASER_ROLE. One deposit therefore cannot be credited under both ids, and no account can move r inside its own sync window. Rounding between the two units is at most one base unit per settle. Three effects remain. First, T is a fixed number while r grows, so the staking yield on the shares that back stHYPE pools and claims stays in the PoolManager and no pool or claim can withdraw it. Second, when the rebaser reports a lower supply, r falls at once (stHYPE.sol lines 400 to 404). T does not change, so paying T now takes more shares than were paid in. If the PoolManager also holds shares for wstHYPE pools, those takes succeed by using them, and the wstHYPE pools end up short by T times the difference of 1/r after and 1/r before. An account that sees the slash coming (the Overseer exposes pendingSlashExists) can deposit under the stHYPE id before the rebase and withdraw after it, and gains that difference on its deposit. Third, pauseTransfer on stHYPE blocks transfer and transferShares, so one pause stops take under both ids.
findings.impact: No funds are exposed today: sharesOf(PoolManager) is zero. If pools or claims exist under both ids, a slash of x percent moves about x percent of the amount owed under the stHYPE id from the LPs of wstHYPE pools to the accounts that withdraw stHYPE first. LPs of stHYPE pools lose the staking yield on their stHYPE, about 2 percent a year at the current rate. A pause freezes every pool that uses either id.
findings.preconditions: Liquidity or claims under both ids in the PoolManager. The loss needs a rebase to a lower supply, which only a holder of REBASER_ROLE can send and which follows a validator slash; Hyperliquid has no automatic slashing at present. The yield loss needs no actor. I did not read the Overseer implementation at 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c, which is not verified on Sourcify. That no public function other than rebase starts a rebase rests on the simulated revert of rebase for an unprivileged caller and on the last rebase transaction.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces and routers on HyperEVM should offer wstHYPE pools only and refuse pools whose currencies include the stHYPE address. LPs should not provide stHYPE through the rebasing contract. The PoolManager cannot call setSelfDisableTransfer on stHYPE with any of its call shapes, so excluding the stHYPE face needs a change in core or a refusal at the interface level. Monitoring should watch stHYPE for Rebase events whose new supply is below the current supply and for TransferPaused.

verification.factCheck: I read the two verified implementations on Sourcify (exact match for both) and reran the chain reads on 2026-11-22 near block 51,966,500. The EIP-1967 slot of stHYPE (0xfFaa4a3D97fE9107Cef8a3F48c069F577Ff76cC1) holds 0xe71caf5c1fe56d8897c7b604295d23968049e057 and that of wstHYPE (0x94e8396e0869c9F2200760aF0621aFd240E1CF38) holds 0x104324863cfb2220756c60384efa9bb67a57aaf7. wstHYPE.sol keeps no balances: balanceOf returns sthype.sharesOf(who) / 1e6 (line 149) and _transfer calls sthype.transferShares(from, to, amount * 1e6) (line 110). stHYPE.sol stores shares, converts with totalSupplyRaw over totalShares (lines 442 to 459), interpolates the supply over syncStart to syncEnd (lines 495 to 513), applies a lower supply at once in syncSupply (lines 400 to 404), restricts syncSupply to REBASER_ROLE (line 394) and blocks transfer and transferShares while transferPaused is set (lines 264 to 288). On chain: stHYPE totalSupply 2,275,416.78, wstHYPE totalSupply 2,192,579.21, ratio 1.03778, balancePerShare 1.037780935902397401, syncEnd minus syncStart 82,800 seconds, rewardsToSync 123.556 HYPE, transferPaused false. sharesOf(PoolManager) and both balanceOf(PoolManager) are zero. rebase() on the Overseer 0xB96f07367e69e86d6e9C3F29215885104813eeAE reverts with AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount (0xe2517d3f) for role 0x5fde63b5...0b75 from an unrelated address and from the PoolManager, and that role value equals keccak256 of REBASER_ROLE. pendingSlashExists() exists and returns false. The issuer page states that the two tokens are two interfaces to the same data, that a transfer of one performs the same action for the other, and warns about multi entry point tokens. The Hyperliquid staking page states that no automatic slashing is implemented at present. I also ran one creation style eth_call that reads stHYPE.balanceOf of a third holder, calls Overseer.mint(address) with 1 HYPE, reads again, calls burnAndRedeemIfPossible and reads again. Both calls succeeded and the holder balance stayed at 106401669038400087184 in all three reads, so a public mint or burn does not move the rate inside one execution. I did not simulate Overseer.redeem(uint256) and the Overseer implementation 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c is not verified, so the statement that only the rebaser can move the rate rests on these simulations and on the role gate in stHYPE.
verification.codeCheck: The PoolManager keys every delta on the pair of caller and currency address (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16 and 28-41) and every claim on uint160 of the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336, src/types/Currency.sol:110-118), so the two token addresses are two unrelated ids. take debits the id it names and calls transfer on that contract (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-87); both contracts return a 32 byte true to the PoolManager for a zero amount transfer, which the success test at Currency.sol:64-74 accepts. A credit is the rise of one balanceOf between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365), the subtraction at line 360 is checked, and one transient slot holds the synced currency (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32), so one deposit of shares gives one credit. I looked for a guard that would stop the loss shift and found none: nothing in src compares the shares held with the sum owed under both ids, and no function reconciles pool state with a token balance. I also looked for an unprivileged variant. The rate is a function of block.timestamp and four storage fields that only syncSupply, mint and burn write, mint and burn keep the rate (stHYPE.sol lines 244 to 256 with the conversion at 442 to 447), and my simulation agrees. The three effects in the finding follow: a fixed stHYPE amount owed while the rate grows leaves yield in the PoolManager, a lower supply makes the same stHYPE amount cost more shares, which a take under the stHYPE id draws from the common share balance, and a pause stops transferShares, which stops wstHYPE transfers as well.
verification.corrections: The actor issuer is correct for the loss shift and for the freeze, since both need a call by a holder of REBASER_ROLE or PAUSER_ROLE, and the slash that would lead to a lower supply is not available to an ordinary account. An ordinary account that deposits under the stHYPE id before such a rebase gains only if that rebase happens. Medium fits because the PoolManager holds neither token today and the loss needs pools or claims under both ids. The statement about slashing is backed by the Hyperliquid staking page, which the finding did not cite.

findings.title: Thirteen Wormhole guardians can act as PoolManager owner on BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche
findings.difference: On Ethereum the owner is the governance timelock itself. On BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche the owner is a Uniswap Wormhole message receiver contract. It executes calls carried in a Wormhole message whose emitter is the Uniswap sender contract on Ethereum. A Wormhole message is valid with 13 of 19 guardian signatures, so the guardian set is a second party that can produce owner calls.
findings.mechanism: 1. owner() of the PoolManager is 0x341c1511141022cf8ee20824ae0ffa3491f1302b on BNB Smart Chain and 0x47eb0cf11a1626462da3c830bcde64c3f582b5a6 on Avalanche. Both contracts carry the strings 'Uniswap Wormhole Message Receiver', 'Invalid Emitter Address!' and 'Sub-call failed', and messageSender() returns 0xf5f4496219f31cdcba6130b5402873624585615a. 2. A message that passes the receiver's checks makes it call arbitrary targets. As owner it can call setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). 3. The controller can set a protocol fee on any pool up to 1000 pips per direction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32) and can withdraw accrued protocol fees to any recipient (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). The withdrawal is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued through a checked subtraction at src/ProtocolFees.sol:55. 4. On BNB Smart Chain the receiver is also owner and feeSetter of the current fee adapter. On Avalanche no controller is set, so the first message through this path would name one. 5. No owner or controller function in src/ reaches pool reserves or ERC-6909 claims. The Owned base contract comes from lib/solmate, which is an empty directory in this checkout, so its transfer function was not read.
findings.impact: Accrued protocol fees and future protocol fees of at most 0.1% of swap input per direction on every pool of the chain. Swappers pay the fee. Liquidity provider principal is not reachable through this path.
findings.preconditions: Thirteen of nineteen Wormhole guardians sign a message that Ethereum governance did not send, or the Wormhole core contract on the chain is compromised. How the receiver verifies signatures, sequence numbers and the 172800 second timeout was inferred from bytecode strings and getters. The receiver source was not read.
findings.mitigations: Monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated and ProtocolFeeUpdated events on both chains and compare them with executed Ethereum governance proposals. Keep accrued protocol fees low by collecting often. Governance can move ownership to a receiver with a second independent attestation if the fee stream grows.
